subsubtopic: SUGGESTED UNILATERAL DECLARATION OF JURISDICTION OVER MARINE RESOURCES TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of increasing evidence that the United States of America is moving steadily toward approving legislation extending its control over ocean fisheries to 200 miles offshore, and despite this nation's other responsibilities and preoccupations in the world scene, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain):
That the Minister of State (Fisheries), the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister of Canada pool their respective courage and resolve and, instructed by this House, at least make a decision to follow the United States in their very logical move to protect that nation's marine resources, since it is obvious that by its indecision, which this government has exhibited on the world scene, no one, particularly the nations with fishing rights, will take seriously any longer Canada's empty and platitudinous pronouncements, and it is only by following as usual in the wake of the United States that we can protect our own fishing industry.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OF SOCIAL CREDIT PRINCIPLES TO COMBAT INFLATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to discuss an important matter of urgent necessity.
Considering that the cost of living has increased in the main urban centres in Canada between May and June, that since June 1964 the cost of living has gone up by 10.6 per cent in the Montreal area alone in comparison with 9.4 per cent in the Quebec City area, and since that staggering rise of prices has reached disastrous proportions threatening to destroy entirely our economy, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
That this House enjoin the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to consider without delay the policies advocated by the Social Credit Party of Canada to put an end to the devastation of inflation and further protect the purchasing power of all Canadian citizens.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member in his concerns about the state of the east coast fishery. However, I believe that my commitment to make a statement in the House or my undertaking to consider making a statement was fully discharged in the full day debate that we had on that question not so long ago and on which subject the House reached a decision. In the meantime, however, we as a government are considering as one of our options for future action the question of unilateral action. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will direct my supplementary question to the Minister of State (Fisheries). In view of the fact that while these ongoing meetings are taking place the fishing industry is deteriorating to a state of oblivion, has the minister had consultation with the Minister of National Defence with regard to stepping up the surveillance capability? subsubtopic: FORCES-ACTION AGAINST FOREIGN VESSELS IGNORING ICNAF QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe there is a mood of total pessimism which has to be questioned. A major company on the east coast last week gave its financial statement for the last quarter, indicating that its profit position came from an improvement in landings. I also have information from some members of this House to the effect that landings in some areas of Newfoundland are good and that some fish are being turned away because the plants cannot process them.
Having said that, I continue to recognize that we must obtain jurisdiction off our shores. To this end, we are pursuing bilateral discussions with a good number of countries. We have already had discussions with the Norwegians, Americans and Mexicans. I would agree that also in the surveillance field we should all live within the rules of ICNAF. That does not mean we cannot increase surveillance. In fact, we have already indicated to National Defence that we desire this to be done.

subtopic: SUGGESTED UNILATERAL JURISDICTION OVER MARINE RESOURCES TO 200 MILES OFFSHORE-EFFECT ON EFFORTS TO CONSERVE FISH STOCKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member must obviously recognize that the current international law is not as he states it to be. The purpose of the negotiations is to change the international law in order to give the coastal states jurisdiction which is not enjoyed by the coastal states at the present time. What the hon. member is saying to me is that we should take the law into our own hands, and at some point it may be necessary to do that. But if it is necessary to do that, I want to be sure that it will bring substantial benefits to Canada and to Canadian fishermen and will not merely lead to simple rhetoric on the day of the announcement.

speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. maintopic: NATURAL GAS-REASON FOR FAILURE OF ENERGY BOARD TO ESTIMATE RESERVES IN MACKENZIE DELTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the board has consistently followed the policy of not establishing estimates for gas fields which are not yet accessible for use within Canada. In particular, it will not regard as reserves that which has not yet been connected up and could be used by consumers. Of course, the board report specifically says that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to hear the hon. member's question, all the more so because when discussing jurisdiction we must not forget there are two oceans, namely the Pacific and the Atlantic. Any oversimplified solution such as "unilateral declaration", which is proposed for demagogical reasons or any other, must take into account the grave implications on salmon which does not recognize jurisdictions be they over 200 miles or elsewhere.
As for the specific question of the hon. member concerning the procedures for the extension of the zones lying between us and the Americans, it goes without saying that this must be considered through bilateral negotiations which are already intricate enough with respect to salmon interception. But I trust that with a friendly country like the United States it will be easy to come to an agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. On Friday last I gave notice that I intended to raise a point of order relating to the answers I had been receiving with regard to the policy of the government on nuclear reactors. I deferred pursuing the point until the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) was back in the House, since he is involved in this question along with the government House leader. On June 27 I questioned the government House leader about the contract with Argentina and I said:
Is it the position of the government that the contract for the Cordoba nuclear generating plant-
That is the Argentinian plant.
-made provision for subsequent negotiation of safeguards-
In reply, the government House leader said:
-the answer to the first part of the question is yes, the contract is subject to a bilateral agreement on safeguards.
Later, on the same day, the same minister said the following:
I am informed there is no doubt about the fact that the fulfilment of the contract itself depends upon a bilateral agreement on adequate safeguards.
In the House, some days later, on July 16, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was asked:
Was there any provision in that contract negotiated with Argentina in 1973 requiring subsequent negotiation of safeguards, other than the agreement to be negotiated with IAEA-
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources replied:
No, sir, that contract was just according to the then general safeguard policy of Canada, namely, the international standard ... the additional standards for the completion of the Argentine contract have been, if you like, unilaterally imposed by Canada at a subsequent date.
Indicating that the answer given to me earlier by the government House leader in his capacity as Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs was clearly misleading. Then the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was asked on July 16, the same day, the following:
-what safeguards the Canadian government is now seeking in respect of this Argentina project?

July 22, 1975

Safeguards which were not in the original contract. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said:
At that time-
In 1973.
-the international standards did not provide for restriction on explosions expressed to be for peaceful rather than weapons purposes. Canada decided as a matter of principle, subsequent to the Indian explosion, to put on a higher level of standards which were set out in the statement I made-
Indicating that the additional safeguard being negotiated with Argentina now is the prohibition of the use of any Canadian facility or reactor or materials provided to Argentina and the restriction that these could not be used by Argentina or by any other country even for peaceful explosions. But I find that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) tabled an exchange of letters which together constitute the contract between Canada and Argentina on September 10, 1974, which reads in part as follows:
In view of Canada's obligations under the Non-Proliferation Treaty, it is Canadian export policy that all material, nuclear material, equipment, facilities and technology supplied from or by Canada will be used only for peaceful purposes and will not in particular be used for the development or manufacture of any nuclear explosive device.
It seems as if this exchange of letters which constituted a supplementary contract back in September of 1974 had already covered the point which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources told us was the sole additional safeguard which Canada is now trying to negotiate with Argentina.
With regard to this Italian business, on July 9 the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources indicated to me in the House, in response to a question, that Canada was retaining a right of veto on any sale which might be made anywhere in the world by the Italian licensee. The minister found he made a mistake and he quickly corrected that. The next day, in response to a question in the House, he told me that any sale made by that Italian licensee would be subject to the Canadian standard of safeguards. That is what the minister said in the House.
Yesterday, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether that was a correct statement which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources had made and he said he did not know, that he would have to verify it. I think there is enough confusion in the nuclear policy of the government already, fundamentally and intrinsically, without more being created by these misleading and evasive answers we have been receiving on this subject.

With respect to the Italian contract, I indicated in the first place that, as I had said on December 20, 1974, of course Atomic Energy of Canada had been authorized to enter into negotiations with the Italian company, that those negotiations are approaching completion, that the company, Atomic Energy, is required to come back to the government with a draft of the proposed agreement to obtain our approval, but that in any event, as stipulated by the safeguards statement on December 20 of last year, any such contract between AECL and the Italian company will be subject to the Canadian safeguard requirements.
In particular, there will be the treaty between the government of Italy and the government of Canada stipulating the limitations imposed upon any Italian company operating within Italy, and also stipulating that in the event of a sale by the Italian company of the Canadian technology to any other country, Italy will be required to get a safeguards agreement of the same standards, including international inspection, as we as Canadians require of the Italians. In other words, for the Italians to be able to licence technology to anyone else, they will have to secure from the buyer exactly the same standards as we secure from them.
In summary, we set up in quite succinct terms the limitations that we as Canadians are going to impose upon the sale of uranium, upon the sale of equipment, including the CANDU reactor, and upon Canadian technology whether or not accompanied by equipment to other states either for their own use or for resale. The restriction is that whether it be for explosive purposes, whether stated by that country, for peaceful purposes or indeed for nonpeaceful purposes, the Canadian equipment, technology and uranium may not be used for that purpose. For this purpose we will seek country to country treaties of the kind tabled by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) to protect this requirement.
A final statement I would make with regard to the Argentine contract is that discussions are proceeding. They are related to further safeguards with respect to reprocessing of the spent fuel from a CANDU reactor within Argentina or the transfer of either spent fuel or technology outside of Argentina to any other country. The completion of that particular requirement of the government of Canada will be precedent to the further performance of Canada under this contract: that negotiations now under way to their successful completion to our satisfaction remains, in our view, a prime condition of our performance, and that nuclear transfers will not go through unless those Canadian standards are met.

In so far as the ministry of Transport is concerned: 1. No written directives on the use of bilge cleaners have been issued to Canadian Coast Guard ships other than by memoranda saying that the amount to be used should be limited to the minimum and bilges should normally be cleaned with hot water and high pressure steam.
2.	The policy is to consider the use of bilge cleaners as coming under the "Steamship Machinery Construction Regulations" which regulate the quantity and manner of stowage of fuel onboard ships.
3.	There are no regulations that specifically refer to toxic bilge cleaners. However, should a cleaner contain a toxic substance which is included in the list of substances in the "Pollutant Substances Regulations", its discharge into the water would be prohibited. The date of proclamation of the "Pollutant Substances Regulations" was February 27, 1973, and notice of this appeared in the Canada Gazette Part II, Volume 107, No. 5.
4.	None at the present time, however, an interdepartmental committee has been formed to study the possibilities of installing containment facilities at several ports.

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE COMPETITIONS OPEN TO MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
1.
Yes. For the purposes of being eligible to enter competitions, members of the Armed Forces are deemed to be employed in the Public Service. However, the Public Service Employment Act requires that, before a closed competition is conducted, the area of competition shall be determined in terms of the part, if any, of the Public Service and the occupational group and level of positions, if any, in which prospective candidates must be employed in order to be eligible for appointment. Therefore a member of the Armed Forces not stationed in the Atlantic Provinces would be eligible to enter closed competitions offered in the Atlantic Provinces, where the competitions have been advertised as open to all employees of the Public Service, employed within geographical limits set, either on a nation-wide basis or so as to include the area in which the member is serving.
2.	Eligibility for appointment, in the case of closed competitions, is normally determined by the positions, or part of the Public Service, in which persons in the Public Service are employed, rather than by the area in which they reside. Therefore, a member of the Armed Forces must continue to retain his status as a serving member and be stationed within the geographical limits prescribed in the area of competition in order to be eligible to compete in a closed competition.
3.	No. A serving member who resigns from the Canadian Armed Forces is ineligible to compete in any closed competition in the Public Service as of the date on which he ceases to be a member of the Armed Forces.

The House resumed, from Monday, July 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-66, to amend the Excise Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stanfield (P. 7416).

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening before the House rose I had been referring to the social and economic condition of our country, a condition brought on by the misrule of the present government which operates under the guise of liberalism. I referred to certain newspaper articles and suggested that the Canadian people, especially those of us who must bear the cost of this misrule, know that Canada is in deep trouble and virtually leaderless.
What is the cause of this, Mr. Speaker? We could go back almost a decade and point to government arrogance, to government abuse of power, to procrastination, especially to the government's misuse of its present majority, to waste of taxpayers' money, poor judgment and chronic indecision. This morning I heard a radio commentator say that the hand is writing on the wall. That reminds me of an old hymn my grandmother used to sing. It is not in the hymn books any more, but it speaks of a story many centuries old, the story of Belshazzar's feast, during which a hand appeared and wrote on the wall and foretold the doom of his government. It goes like this;
At the feast of Belshazzar,
And a thousand of his Lords,
How they drank of golden vessels,
As the book of truth records.
In the night as they revelled,
In the lordly palace hall,
They were seized with consternation,
By the hand upon the wall.
How true it is today. The government is a perfect example of that to which the hymn refers, the hymn which my Scottish grandmother used to sing almost a century ago. The hand is writing on the wall for the government because, as the Scriptures say, they were weighed in the balance and found wanting. The Medes and the Persians are at the gates. I shall make no more metaphors; this will be the last. But the modern Medes and Persians are inflation and unemployment.
We have the spectacle before us of a government which imposes a ten cents a gallon surtax on gasoline and, in the same stroke of the pen, removes the tax from wine. That is one for the books. The government wants to tax the daylights out of those who need gasoline to make a living, and says to them, "Drink more wine and you won't feel the pain." I really don't know whether the minister was thinking about the true connoisseur when he removed the tax on wine, or if he was trying to ease the lot of the poor who feel the pinch of inflation. I think someone is greasing the skids under the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). He
Excise Tax Act
accepted poor advice when he lumped these two measures in one bill. Imagine including wine and gasoline in one bill! One cannot help comparing what has been done to wine with what has been done to gasoline.
I should hate to see the minister ridden out of the House by his colleagues, because that will be the effect of this bill. Personally, I shall hate to see him go. I have come to enjoy looking at his pleasant face across the floor and having the occasional exchange of banter and repartee. The minister is an interesting man and a rather pleasant sort; he is a good Canadian, too. But he was been badly misled. I think someone in his department was putting him on by drafting a bill like C-66 and asking him to put his stamp of approval on it.
Reading this bill we come across another anomaly, proposed section 17 on page 5. The proposed section reads:
Thermal insulation materials designed exclusively for insulation of buildings; storm doors and storm windows for buildings; articles and materials for use exclusively in the manufacture or production thereof.
I was in the building materials and lumber business for 25 years, and in my opinion this proposed section will invite arbitrary interpretation by bureaucratic bunglers as to what actually constitutes insulating materials. Lumber is an insulating material, as is paper, glass, concrete, brick, stone and scores of other materials. They are, to a varied degree, insulators. To carry this argument further, the whole purpose of a building is to insulate the occupants and appurtenances from the weather. Every single material or substance can, in some instances, be considered as an insulating material. Why did not the drafters of this monstrous document simply say that all building materials are hereafter exempt from federal taxes?
Hear, hear!

Every speaker, excepting the two or three government supporters who took part in this debate, made the point I have just made. I can suggest a number of reasons why federal taxes should be taken off building materials completely and immediately. The main reason, of course, is the slump in housing starts in Canada. The slump has come exactly when thousands of new dwelling units are desperately needed. At the same time, the minister of state responsible for housing says that there is no way he can meet his own projections this year for housing starts. His is a sad case. If the federal government is truly concerned about housing starts, it should take the reasonable and logical step of taking the tax off building materials and then appoint a minister of housing who can get the show on the road.
Another reason for removing the tax on building materials is that the United States market for Canadian lumber is thinning because of a decline of housing starts in that country. A number of lumber companies in British Columbia have closed owing to a slump in the market. This would be a good time to put that surplus lumber to work. It could be used for the building of homes for Canadians. We should do everything we can to accomplish that end. Including clauses like proposed section 17 in tax bills is not the way to do it, Mr. Speaker. We do not need any more of that hard to interpret gobbledygook on the statute books. There is too much of it already and it accomplishes no good purpose.

July 22, 1975
Excise Tax Act
Also, I should have to see the finance minister railroaded out of the House by his colleagues because he has become master of the one-liner since assuming his present cabinet responsibilities. Some of his lines are real gems. Take, for instance, his statement in the budget speech a few days ago. He said the government found it necessary to steer a narrow course between inflation and unemployment. He should get a prize for that one. What he really meant was that the government was threading its way among the multitude of problems facing the country and so far they have managed to avoid making contact with any of the problems.
I have read some startling accounts in the press lately, and again today, about the incredible mismanagement of Air Canada. Although I share the concern of the average Canadian about this appalling state of affairs, I am not surprised. The former Auditor General, Maxwell Henderson, warned us for years that the country was being as badly managed as Air Canada and other Crown corporations. The same crowd is responsible for fiscal and management policies. No wonder the national budget for the present fiscal year is close to $30 billion. It could be much higher before the year is out. No wonder the government is scratching the bottom of the barrel, trying to find new sources of revenue. Thus, of course, the ten-cent gasoline tax. They are invading a provincial field, although there is nothing in Canadian law to prevent their so doing.
A couple of weeks ago some of the spokesmen in the higher echelons of the Liberal Party said that if Ontario does not like the ten-cent additional gasoline tax being levied at the pumps, why do they not take off the provincial tax? What colossal nerve and affrontery! Ontario has a 19-cent a gallon gasoline tax. This revenue is used to build and maintain highways. They have been doing a good job. The federal government has a lot of nerve asking the Ontario government to vacate in part a field which they have historically held, in order to make room for this illegitimate affrontery to raise more revenue for the Trudeau government. We are in that position today.
The present government has got itself boxed in. That is the reason for levying this tax. It cannot restrain itself now because the habit of spending recklessly has become too deeply entrenched. It is far easier to get into a bad habit than to kick one. I do not believe this government is interested in kicking its habit of overspending. Liberal cabinet ministers have had access to the public purse for too long to give up this largesse. In fact, it is obvious they want more money to spend on their personal programs and projects. When they are called upon to solve serious problems, their first thought is to spend their way out of them. When they find themselves short of cash, they send their friendly Minister of Finance on a foraging expedition. In this bill we find him poaching in the traditional domain of the provinces. We find him gouging taxes from the retail sale of gasoline which traditionally have been left to the provinces for the construction and maintenance of roads and highways.
The minister got off another good one-liner when the Premier of Ontario objected to the imposition of the tencent a gallon increase in the surtax. The minister suggested that if the premier thought the price of gasoline was too

high, he could drop the 19-cent a gallon Ontario tax on gasoline. I can see the premier setting up the province for another federal kill. If Premier Davis were to drop the 19-cent tax, the finance minister and his cronies would jump in like a flock of vultures, saying that if the province did not want the 19 cents, the federal government would take it.
It looks as though there will be another injustice perpetrated on the Canadian taxpayers in connection with this legislation. That is on the question of rebates returned by the government to those who have purchased and burned gasoline in the course of earning their livelihood and in necessary travel to and from their jobs. At first it was reported that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bas-ford) had stated that the ten cents a gallon rebate would not be taxable. Now that has been contradicted by his department and they say that the rebate will be taxed. If this is so, it is a glaring, rank injustice. I do not believe that ruling would be upheld in a court of law. This would be absolute theft on the part of the government theft from the taxpayers.
First, the money that he or she earned as income in order to buy gasoline is taxed. Then they take some of it to buy a tank of gasoline to go to work and pay the ten-cent per gallon tax, which then is rebated to them at a later date in full. If the government taxes that rebate, it will be double taxation. Moreover, it will be taxation of amounts that have nothing to do with income. How crazy can the government get? This legislation is shaky enough without compounding it with such nonsense. I say to the Minister of Finance and to the Minister of National Revenue, make a non-taxing return of the gasoline tax to the industrial and workaday users. Do that and you will be in the better books of the Canadian taxpayers, which you are not at the present time.
The Minister of Finance has said he is taxing gasoline users ten cents per gallon, plus the wellhead crude oil tax, and is doing this for revenue purposes. I wonder for what specific purposes. The Trudeau record under the guise of liberalism is a sorry mess. The minister says, of course, that the first purpose is to subsidize the extra cost of gasoline and oil in the eastern part of our country, but he also stated in his speech on July 9 that this item will bolster the consolidated revenue fund. That is why I ask the question that this House and all of Canada is asking: For what will the $500 million a year be used?
Some questions immediately arise. Will this be used to finance more give away programs? Will it be used to finance CIDA's colossal expenditures in foreign countries? I am not the red-necked bigot that a Liberal would try to label me. Some of these projects are legitimate for our purpose of being a world nation trying to help our brothers, but a good share of it is nothing but extravagance and wasted money. Will this revenue be used to finance the self-indulgent extravagances of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)? No answer there. Will it be used to finance deficits created by bad deals and judgments such as Microsystems, not far from Ottawa, which in the name of liberalism was given a $30 million grant? That was a big one, Mr. Speaker. That is another failure of "Trudeaucracy".
July 22, 1975

There is an example of a smaller loss in my constituency. Even though it is small, prorated it is as important as the $30 million poured down the drain just outside this city. Just before the 1972 election, one of the candidates for the Liberal nomination announced they had made a grant to a lathe mill in Northbrook of over $6,000, supposedly to train machine operators. A month after the grant was announced, the firm went out of business and no operators were trained or needed. The site is on the outskirts of the village along Highway 41 and is a public nuisance and eyesore, with its huge pile of edgings and dilapidated buildings with junk piled around.
That is all that is left of another Liberal grant. Moreover, it is a regional fire hazard. The government will be hearing more about this from me because the mess has to be cleaned up; it is detrimental to our countryside. We are trying to attract tourists. They do not come here to seek junk, edging piles and fire hazards. Government spending is a bottomless pit to which it consigns the taxpayers' earnings.
As the finance minister steers his narrow course between inflation and unemployment, I hope he will take the trouble to look to the right and to the left, up and down, and forward and backward. If he will just do that, he will see where he is going. We are drifting along in so many directions at this time that I am surprised the finance minister would even suggest that this sort of meandering can be described as steering a narrow course. It is more like the narrow course the legendary bull charted through the china shop. Like the china shop, the country is in a shamble, and it would appear that the worst is yet to come. If the government is getting so short of funds and sources of additional revenue as to transgress into provincial tax preserves, then we must be in serious economic straits indeed; much worse, I would suspect, than the finance minister has told us.
I must also join my hon. friends in protesting the manner in which the Minister of Finance imposed this increase in the excise tax-by an announcement in the middle of a speech in the House. This is taxation by fiat and is further evidence that the government has no ethics about tabling tax legislation before the fact; it has found it is more convenient and expeditious to table legislation after the tax has been imposed and after it has come into force. This is contrary to the rule of law and contrary to the tradition followed by all the governments which preceded the would-be dictators across the floor.
What are some of the exemptions for which the bill provides? Section 2 refers to air travel. All non-Canadians using commercial air travel from points outside our country are excluded. But all Canadians emplaning from points within Canada will pay. The excise tax on wine has been sharply cut. All users of Canadian wine will from now on pay only 2lA cents tax per gallon, instead of 20 cents a gallon as formerly, if the alcoholic content is 7 per cent or less, and only five cents per gallon instead of 40 cents per gallon on wine with an alcohol content of more than 7 per cent.
I note, also, that the tax has been removed from insulation materials, incidentally, this measure should benefit
Excise Tax Act
all those people who buy insulating materials as a means of keeping their wine cold. Persons exempted from tax include Her Majesty in right of Canada, an exemption which extends to the Prime Minister and covers his Liberal picnic junkets around the country in armed forces' helicopters. But the working man has no exemptions whatsoever.
I wish to speak briefly as a member with three prisons in his riding, each of which has been a continuing source of trouble to the community and to the country. I ask the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) why it was considered necessary or expedient to cut back the proposed prison construction program touted for so long. If the revenue to be raised by this tax was to be used to build new prisons or to modernize old prisons, I might be inclined to accept it with some grace. However, as has already been pointed out by many of my hon. friends, the money to be collected is to go into general revenues; it will not be used to build roads or prisons or to create jobs or fight inflation. In fact, on the contrary, it will only serve to feed the fires of inflation.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) suggested last week that we in the official opposition would be pleased to lend the services of our esteemed economic critic, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) to help the Minister of Finance. Our economic critic could remind him of what he has said in the past concerning the state of our economic health. He could remind him how wide of the mark he has been with his predictions and projections. He might even be able to advise him how to get out of the mess in which his cabinet colleagues have placed him.
The minister is being roasted by his own colleagues and he will be cast aside as soon as it suits the purposes of those who constitute the real power of liberalism. I extend an invitation to the minister to come over to this side of the House when his colleagues are finished with him. He will have to start at the bottom and learn his craft, but there might be a better future for him in a party which places a higher value on service and honour than on power for the sake of power.
If the government is sincere about reducing expenditures, it could begin by withdrawing the hundreds of millions it is squandering each year on the so-called bilingualism program in the public service. That program has become a scandalous, expensive disaster and instead of promoting bilingualism it is being used to promote racism. Those of us who complain about the way in which the program has deteriorated into a scheme to recruit and promote public servants on the basis of race are called racists, but it is becoming apparent to the majority of Canadians that this is simply a smokescreen thrown up by those who hope they can obscure the truth about what is happening.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As a fellow parliamentarian, I respect your judgment. However, I would draw to your attention the fact that the bill pertains to finance; it pertains to revenue. I mentioned the government's bilingualism program and the inefficiency with which it is being carried out because it has a direct bearing on expenditure, on the nation's financial affairs. This led me to refer to the protest raised by the Association of Protestant School Boards in Quebec which is asking for a ruling on the Quebec official languages act, Bill 22, on the grounds that it will constitute a hardship to some of the citizens of that province.
If hon. members care to look at today's Ottawa Journal, they will find a headline reading "Trudeau rules out Bill 22 challenge". Hail, the just society!
Get back to the bill.

However, as I say, Mr. Speaker, I respect your ruling. On the admission of both the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) and the chairman of the Public Service Commission, the commission intends to ignore the merit system in recruiting for the public service until it is satisfied there is a ratio among employees roughly equivalent to the population ratio of English and French Canadians. This practice is against federal regulations, it is against provincial regulations and it is against all the rules of decent conduct in our society. That is liberalism for you. This is the Trudeau just society.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Penner).]
At a time when we are trying to wipe out all traces of discrimination on the basis of race, creed, colour, religion or national origin, this government is promoting racism, and in the process is trying to turn the two founding cultures and races of our country into opposing camps. This is a strange method indeed for a government to promote unity in a country where people have been getting along so well for generations.
The finance minister has freely admitted that the ten cents a gallon tax to be levied on motorist and gasoline users at the retail level is to be used by the government for badly needed revenue purposes, and it is estimated this revenue will total $500 million per year. I have referred to their bad habits of the past, and these are coming home to haunt the government. There is an old French saying out of everyday human experience that certainly applies here, and it is this: "Plus qu'hier, moins que demain". In English, it means the more yesterday, the less tomorrow. In other words, the more you spent and dissipated yesterday, the less you have for tomorrow. Is that not true, Mr. Speaker?
The Trudeau government wasted and squandered so much yesterday, in the past, that the outlook for tomorrow is fraught with financial difficulties of their own making; and as I previously stated, they are weighed in the balance and found wanting.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first to acknowledge your ruling that the remarks of hon. members should be relevant to the bill under consideration. As Your Honour knows, Bill C-66 imposes a gasoline excise tax of ten cents a gallon on gasoline sold by refiners and importers of gasoline. The tax is not imposed on the sale of diesel fuel, aviation fuel and heating fuel. I want to observe your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and to deal with the technical administration of the proposed tax. The policy reasons behind this measure were, I think, eloquently and cogently put by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in his budget statement and speech on moving second reading of this bill, and in the exceedingly fine speech of my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald).
In following the course of the debate on second reading of this bill, some hon. members have raised questions on the administrative aspects of the proposed gasoline excise tax and I hope they would be interested in some enlightenment on the subject this afternoon. Notwithstanding that this tax is expected to generate some $350 million in the remaining portion of this fiscal year, the cost of collection of this large sum will be minimal since the 20 refiners and 10 gasoline importers affected by payment of the tax already pay sales tax to the Department of National Revenue each month in the regular course of their business. So they will only be required to make minor adjustments in their accounting system to record and remit the gasoline excise tax. This is provided for in the bill, and these 20 refiners and 10 importers will simply add the proposed gasoline tax to that remission.
Furthermore, in terms of the administration of the refund programs, even though it is expected that upwards of one million persons will be entitled to claim refunds of
July 22, 1975

gasoline tax as a relieving measure, the cost of the collection and processing of refund claims will be about 1 per cent. This is in the same range as the present administration costs of the general manufacturers sales tax that is currently in place.
The administration is being geared, on passage of the bill, to refund the tax on gasoline provided for in the bill, gasoline that is used for commercial purposes by delivery trucks, buses, taxis, construction equipment, manufacturing equipment, mining and forestry equipment, by farmers, commercial fishermen and hunters and trappers who use gasoline in the course of farming, commercial fishing, hunting and trapping activities.
Tax relief will also be provided by way of refunds to hospitals, federal and provincial government departments and agencies, as well as to persons who claim a portion of their vehicle expenses as a deduction against income tax in computing their income. Hon. members know that this will include doctors, commercial travellers, salesmen, business people using their cars in the course of their business, self-employed professional persons, manufacturers, retailers, hospitals and day-care centres when the gasoline is used in their vehicles and equipment.
Generally then, Mr. Speaker, with the bill as now proposed and reprinted by order of Your Honour, all persons who use gasoline in the course of their business or commercial activities for the purpose of earning income will be entitled to claim a refund as well as those manufacturers who are exempt from the 12 per cent federal sales tax on gas purchased for further manufacture. Also, the refund of the gasoline tax is not limited to gasoline purchased for cars, trucks and other vehicles; it will also be allowed for use in snowmobiles, tractors, lawn mowers and motor boats if the gasoline was consumed for business or for income-producing purposes.
As the House knows, originally Bill C-66 contained section 47(1)(f) providing for payment of the refund to a large group of persons and organizations not required to pay income tax on their earnings. That list, provided in the Income Tax Act, includes such bodies as municipal authorities or public bodies performing a similar function, school boards, municipal and provincial corporations, charitable organizations, non-profit organizations, charitable trusts, trade unions or labour organizations, housing corporations within the meaning of that expression as defined by the National Housing Act, and others. Without in any way reflecting on Your Honour's ruling in this instance, I would hope that at the committee stage of the bill the House would be amenable to suggestions to be made by the Minister of Finance to bring back into the bill relief from this tax for a group of non-business users of gasoline.
Dealing further with the administration of this proposed tax, employers who pay a mileage allowance to their employees for business travel will be allowed to claim a refund either on the basis of ten cents per gallon for actual gasoline expended in business travel or the employer will be permitted a factor of a fraction of a cent per mile. I propose to recommend to the governor in council on passage of the bill that a factor of five-eighths of a cent per mile be authorized for calculation by an employer who paid his employee mileage. As may be evident, the intent
Excise Tax Act
of the proposed legislation is to exempt all users of gasoline other than those who use gasoline for personal transportation or other personal use.
There will also be situations where gasoline is consumed in vehicles that are used partly for business and partly for pleasure. In situations of this kind, only that portion of gasoline which is consumed when the vehicle is being used for business purposes or for income-producing purposes will be subject to the refund.
How would you measure that?

I will come to the point the hon. member has just raised in a few moments. For example, in a situation where an eligible person, say a doctor or salesman, drove an automobile 20,000 miles in a year, where only 12,000 miles or 60 per cent was on commercial business, that person would have paid a total of $125 of gasoline excise tax if he had purchased 1,250 gallons of gasoline, and he would be entitled to a gasoline refund of $75.
The hon. member has asked how we would calculate that, how we would administer it. This type of assessment, this type of judgment or this type of arrangement is already in place and made under the existing Income Tax Act where people are entitled to deduct a certain proportion of their vehicle expense for tax purposes.
I will come to the point raised by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) in a moment. The hon. member for Peace River raised a question the other day with which I shall deal later. I emphasize that while no claim for refund can be paid before the bill receives royal assent, when and if it does provision will be made for large refund claims to be made on a monthly basis and reimbursement should be made within two or three weeks of receipt of the claim.

On the basis of that, Mr. Speaker, as I say- to re-emphasize-refund claims of $200 will be received and paid monthly and those of less than $200 will be accepted twice a year. The smaller claims will be accepted on or after December 31, 1975. To give some indication of the magnitude of the claims involved, we estimate, for example, that a commercial salesman travels between
20.000	and 40,000 business miles per year, and also that a taxicab travels approximately 100,000 to 150,000 business miles per year.
Using that calculation related to a car which travels an average 16 miles to the gallon, we find that the commercial salesman would receive a refund of between $125 and $250 per year, and that the taxi driver would receive between $625 and $937.50 per year. Dealing with the exemption for eastern farmers, the average eastern farmer burns 3,000 gallons of gasoline per year on farming. His refund would be about $300 per year. The average western farmer burns
1.000	gallons of gasoline per year, which is less than his eastern counterpart because western farmers use diesel engines to a greater extent. This represents a rebate of $100. I have asked for statistics relating to fishermen and the amount of the refund anticipated for them, but because of the very diverse nature of the fishing industry it is extremely difficult to draw out what would be a meaningful average.
The method of payment of refunds that we propose to space out monthly, semi-annually and annually will, I want to reassure the hon. member for Peace River who raised this matter, in fact help stabilize the work load in the data centre where these refund claims will be handled. At the present time, the data centre is used to process income tax returns. We have a peak load at tax filing time. The high load then falls off, and the administration throughout the year of the gasoline tax refund program would stabilize employment within the data centre and solve some of our administrative problems.
Some hon. members opposite have raised the question of administration. I wish to draw it to their attention that, for example, the present program of refunds under the Income Tax Act, as an average, on a correct return requires a period of five weeks from the time of receipt of the return until payment by the Department of Supply and Services. Obviously, the processing of a rather simple form relating to the gasoline tax is a far simpler task than the assessment and processing of an income tax return; therefore, the time spent on these refunds should be considerably less than the time spent on income tax returns.
Since no refund of the gasoline excise tax is permitted for personal use, my department will not refund tax for mileage which the employer might pay his employee for travel from his home to his place of work since this is

comparable to the personal expenses of a person travelling from his home to his place of employment. Furthermore, a lawyer, medical doctor or business person using his car to drive from his home to his place of business would similarly be unable to claim refund of the gasoline tax for that travel.
It goes without saying that my department will not condone-I think this is a point that was raised by one hon. member-fraudulent claims and will consider prosecution in those instances which are uncovered by auditors during their periodic review of claimants' records. This mechanism is already in place in my department in assessing and auditing present tax returns.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the status of the gasoline excise tax refunds for purposes of the Income Tax Act. It will be recognized, of course, that a person is only entitled to claim his net cost as an expense for tax purposes. If, therefore, he charges as expense the full price of the gasoline, including the ten cents per gallon to be rebated, he must add the rebate into his declared income. If, on the other hand, he charges only his net expense, excluding the rebate, he would need to take no further steps regarding income tax in respect of the rebate when he receives it.
In view of the comments, I might add a little more in explanation of that situation. The Income Tax Act provides for two methods of computing income and expenses-the cash method and the accrual method. In brief, the cash method must be used by taxpayers whose income is derived from office or employment, including commission salesmen. Farmers and fishermen may elect to use this method or the accrual method. The income of all other businesses, including the professions, must be reported on the accrual basis.
Under the cash method, income is reported in the year it is received and expenses are deducted in the year they are paid. Consequently, an individual using this basis will be entitled to deduct the total amount paid during the year for the gasoline purchased for business purposes, and report as income the gasoline tax rebate actually received during the year. As an alternative, he may reduce the gasoline purchases by the amount of the rebate and claim only the net cost of the gasoline as an expense. For example, if his gasoline purchases amounted to $700 and he received a rebate of $100, he could either claim the $700 as an expense and report the $100 rebate as income, or claim the net amount which is $600. The over-all effect for tax purposes is the same.
Under the accrual method, income is reported in the year it is earned, regardless of when the payment is actually received. In turn, expenses are deductible in the year incurred, whether paid or unpaid. Therefore, a taxpayer using this method will claim the net cost of gasoline, that is, the total gasoline purchased reduced by the rebates applicable to those purchases.
I wish to assure the House, particularly the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), that the administration of this tax will not be an administrative nightmare as was suggested by him in the House. My department has made arrangements for refund claims on the basis of the passage
July 22, 1975

of the bill, and contingency planning for forms, for instruction sheets and for self-addressed return envelopes to be available at all excise offices, customs offices and post offices across Canada shortly after Labour Day-on the basis of the passage of the bill in the current month.
These forms, if completed in accordance with the detailed instructions on the back, will be processed by the existing computer taxation data centre in Ottawa, using the special program developed specifically for the processing of gasoline claims, without delay. I have given the times when they will be paid and the schedule in the year. When the bill is passed, I urge each claimant to take care in completing the form, which is to be a simple one, follow the instructions and then his refund will be paid in the time periods I have set up.
Frankly, I am pleased with the organization that my department has put in place for contingency planning in anticipation of the passage of Bill C-66. My officials are ready to proceed with the administration of the gasoline tax refund program. It is not the kind of administrative problem that the Leader of the Opposition suggested it would be.
It sure is for the public.

The form is designed so as to be easy to complete and yet provides my department with the minimal required information for compliance purposes. I emphasize, for those who have said it is difficult for the taxpayers, that we will not normally ask persons to send in their gasoline invoices with their claims, but will accept a declaration that the information given is accurate.
Oh, oh!
Unlike the opposition, we have faith in the Canadian public.
Hear, hear!
But they don't have faith in you.

However, claimants will be required to keep on hand documentary evidence of the purchase for audit by members of the Department of National Revenue in the event that there are a few cheaters, which members of the opposition seem to think there are in Canada.
I would merely recommend, and I do so on the basis that Bill C-66 is like all measures that have preceded it, contrary to what the hon. member for Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack) said, that anyone who uses gasoline at this time for commercial purposes maintains a careful record of his gasoline purchases, particularly gasoline used for business, to enable him to file his claim as soon as passage of the bill and distribution of the forms are completed.
I am confident that the present excise organization and the existing data centre in Ottawa will be able to handle the processing of gasoline tax refund claims promptly and efficiently and without undue inconvenience to the general public. It must be obvious to members of the House that, contrary to the comments made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), my department has this matter of the administration of the gasoline tax well in
Excise Tax Act
hand and will be proceeding, following the passage of the bill, with the issuance of refunds in an orderly and expeditious manner as outlined in my remarks today.
I want to conclude by referring to the comments made by the hon. member for Peace River when he said we could commence to pay out the refunds without passage of the bill. That is not correct. I presume that what was being referred to when the question was raised in the House is that the claimant could use section 17 of the Financial Administration Act for the purpose of claiming the remittance of the special excise tax on gasoline. That is the section which allows the governor in council to make remissions. Presumably, what was suggested by the hon. member for Peace River is an order in council under that provision, remitting the tax to the purchasers described in new section 47, clause 5 of the bill. I hesitate to disagree with the hon. member for Peace River who is the opposition House leader, a distinguished member and parliamentarian. I am only a humble minister. But I am bound by the advice I receive from the law officers of the Crown.
I am also conscious of the fact that I have to run my department in accordance with the rules of the Financial Administration Act. I have always endeavoured to run the departments which I have headed so as not to receive adverse comments from the Auditor General. Therefore, I must regretfully decline the invitation of the hon. member for Peace River to pay the refunds before the passage of the bill. The fact is that such an arrangement would be illegal and impossible. A remission order under section 17 of the Financial Administration Act cannot be used for the purpose suggested, namely, that of paying the refunds before the passage of the bill. A remission order under that provision may only be made in the case of a tax as defined in section 17(10) of the Financial Administration Act which defines a tax as being, among other things, a tax "payable to Her Majesty imposed or authorized to be imposed by any Act of Parliament". Until such time as Bill C-66 is enacted into law, there is no special excise tax on gasoline authorized by parliament.
What an absurdity!

Let me say to a group of members who always claim to be conscious of the rules of parliament and who insist that the government should observe the rules, that I emphasize that this bill has not been passed. As provided in section 17 of the Financial Administration Act, we could only refund a tax that had been authorized or imposed by an act of parliament. On the other hand, it is in accordance with a well established tradition of this government, and of Conservative governments the few times they have been in office, that the amount can be collected from the time of the tabling of the ways and means motion, because when finally enacted into law, as I mentioned earlier, the bill and the tax will be retroactive to that date.
The second suggestion of the hon. member for Peace River is not workable because, in any event, the Financial Administration Act which provides for a remission order cf a tax authorized by parliament only provides for the remission of that tax to the taxpayer, namely, to the person upon whom the tax has been imposed. As I made clear in my opening remarks, the tax under Bill C-66 is

July 22, 1975
Excise Tax Act
imposed on 20 refiners and 10 importers. I do not think the hon. member for Peace River is suggesting that we refund the tax to those 30 taxpayers, and yet those are the only taxpayers entitled to a remission under the Financial Administration Act.
The scheme under Bill C-66 is quite different from what the hon. member for Peace River envisages. It is not a refund of the tax to those 30 taxpayers but, rather, a refund of an amount equal to the tax payable to the purchaser of gasoline on which the tax has already been paid. The scheme of the bill is to provide relief by way of a refund to a group of people who have purchased gasoline. However, under the bill and under the Financial Administration Act that amount is not to be refunded to the taxpayers whom I pointed out, namely, the manufacturer, producer or importer of gasoline.
Much as I would like to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Peace River that we pay out the refunds regardless of what parliament does and whether the bill is passed or not, which seems to be what he is saying, from the best advice I have from the law officers of the Crown and from my desire to run my department in accordance with practice which would not lead to adverse comment from the Auditor General, it is a scheme and an invitation which I cannot accept.

Mr. Speaker, some time ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told the people of Canada that he would wrestle inflation to the ground. The budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) of June 23 and the legislation which will proceed from it, including Bill C-66 which we are now discussing and which imposes a ten-cent per gallon excise tax on gasoline, provide the people of this country with an excellent opportunity to see who is going to do the battling in this well orchestrated wrestling match. Whenever a Liberal government, whether in peacetime or wartime, calls upon the Canadian people to make sacrifices, one can always be sure that the sacrifices will be borne by the people least able to carry them. In this fight against inflation the burden will be carried by the victims of inflation and not by the beneficiaries.
An old Liberal tradition.

It will come as no surprise to anyone that the corporate sector of this country will benefit very materially. It has already benefited by the previous budgets of the present Minister
Excise Tax Act
of Finance by means of rapid write-offs and accelerated depreciation which have given the corporate sector in the neighbourhood of $2 billion, and in the present budget it again does very well. It is benefiting to the tune of some $240 million, $200 million in tax credits and an additional $40 million through changes in the resource industry tax legislation. If, in the endeavour to wrestle inflation to the ground, somebody has to tighten their belt, it is apparently not going to be the corporate elite; they are going to be allowed to view the battle from afar.
*
Under this legislation and the related bills announced in the budget, the battle against inflation will be fought by those who must drive a car to work, by the employees who will have to pay higher unemployment insurance premiums, and by those who are unfortunate enough to be ill or bedridden.
Let me deal, first of all, with the increase in energy costs, particularly oil and natural gas. This budget will add to the energy costs of the Canadian consumer some $2 billion per year. The bill we are now discussing imposes a ten-cent gasoline excise tax at the wholesale level. By the time it reaches the retail level it will probably be in the neighbourhood of 12 cents per gallon. The $1.50 per barrel increase in the price of crude oil is imposed at the wellhead. By the time it reaches the gasoline pump it will probably be an increase of six or eight cents per gallon. Between the excise tax and the increase in the price of oil there has been added to gasoline, in all probability, 18 to 20 cents per gallon by the time the full effect of the present measures comes into operation.
It is true, as the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) pointed out this afternoon, that fishermen, farmers, construction contractors and manufacturers will get refunds. He also pointed out that professional groups such as doctors, lawyers, dentists and self-employed persons such as salesmen, insurance agents, real estate agents and other self-employed businessmen will be able to deduct this additional cost under the Income Tax Act.
The minister's statement this afternoon makes it perfectly clear, however, that the one group that will have no recourse whatsoever is the workers who have to drive a considerable distance to work. As a matter of fact, the minister went out of his way to point out that if an employer pays the expenses of an employee travelling to work, that will not be deductible. Money spent by a salesman or a professional person carrying on his or her legitimate business will be deductible, but there is no way by which a worker who will have this additional burden imposed upon him will be able to deduct it or get a refund.
I suppose one can understand that a government which is mainly associated with people who live in cities and metropolitan areas who think of driving as a luxury or pleasure, fails to recognize that there are thousands of small towns and hundreds of small cities and rural areas in this country where people live a long way from their place of employment.
In my constituency, workers who live in the small cities of Nanaimo and Duncan drive 30 to 50 miles to a sawmill, pulpmill or logging camp. There are longshoremen who live in Ladysmith and Nanaimo who are on call to go to a

July 22, 1975
Excise Tax Act
port anywhere on Vancouver Island. That can involve a trip of 50 to 70 miles return. Yet there is no way in which they can charge off the additional cost of them as a result of this tax. The use of a car is not a luxury for them; it is a necessity. There is no way under the program and the detail which the Minister of Revenue announced this afternoon by which these workers will be able to pass on to anybody the additional cost in the price of gasoline.
If business or professional people have increased costs, they can pass them on as legitimate costs of their operation, but the workers cannot do that. The worker is limited to the normal $150 per year deduction for expenses, which is just as applicable to a bank clerk who does not have to buy tools other than a ballpoint pen and who has only to catch a bus. People whose travelling expenses will amount to hundreds of dollars per year will have to pay the extra cost out of their present income. Therefore, they will either have to lower their standard of living or demand higher wages. If they demand higher wages, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance will hold them up to the public as the main cause of inflation in this country.
The government has put forward three arguments to justify this ten cents per gallon increase for gasoline and the $1.50 per barrel increase in the price of oil which, as I pointed out, will cost the average consumer who drives a car anywhere from 18 to 20 cents per gallon. The first argument they put up is that raising the price will have the effect of reducing consumption. They tell us this was a conservation measure. As a matter of fact, Madam Speaker, all the evidence that can be procured indicates that rationing by the pocketbook has never reduced consumption. Take oil as an example. The price of a barrel of oil, from 1971 to 1975, increased from $2.90 to $6.50; that is, more than a 100 per cent increase, and it has been reflected in the increased price of gasoline. Has there been a corresponding reduction in consumption? No. As a matter of fact, consumption of gasoline in that same period rose by over 12 per cent. As a conservation measure, therefore, the increase in the price of gasoline and other fuels is not a remedy.
The second argument is that the government needs the ten cents per gallon in order to net $350 million this year- in a full fiscal year it will net much more-because they want to maintain a uniform price for gasoline across the country, and since there will be a deficit in the oil compensation payments this is the way to meet that deficit. Up until now the export tax has brought the government sufficient revenue to more than pay for the import compensation costs. This year the government thinks it will face a deficit-and it probably will-and therefore it is going to recoup its loss by placing this ten cents per gallon tax on gasoline.
I should like to point out that part of this $350 million could be secured by a much more rigid scrutiny of oil compensation payments to the oil companies. There is growing evidence that the oil companies have been ripping off the oil compensation fund and that they have been switching their deliveries of oil from high-price areas to low-price areas to enable them to collect the compensation payments and use the cheaper oil in other areas.

Remember, we are not dealing with a few Canadian companies; we are dealing with the great multinational corporations which control 90 per cent of oil production in Canada, 99 per cent of oil refining in Canada and which can ship oil around the world to wherever they choose. They have deliberately manipulated oil imports to get the maximum out of the oil compensation fund. The government could save some money in that area.
If it is necessary to raise money in order to meet a deficit in the oil compensation fund, surely it ought to be collected on the basis of ability to pay. I heard some Liberal members argue that they did not want to see this deficit made up by increasing the income tax, since we should be taxing people who do not drive cars. There is a simple answer to that. If the government wants to raise this $350 million a year, it could impose an income surcharge on incomes above a certain level. Certainly, when you deal with the middle and higher income groups you are dealing with people who own cars and operate one, two or even more cars.
Do not forget corporation taxes.

As my
colleague suggests, there is nothing to prevent the government imposing a small surcharge on this country's corporations in order to raise money and meet any deficit in the oil compensation fund. But the government did not choose either of those courses. It is not prepared to tax more heavily the comfortably well-off, nor the corporations. Instead, it puts on a flat tax of ten cents a gallon which everyone who drives a car must pay, including those who must drive in order to hold down a job. To me that is scandalous.
The third argument put forward by the government for imposing this gasoline tax and also for raising the price of oil from $6.50 per barrel to $8 per barrel is this: the government and the oil industry need the money in order to find oil and natural gas supplies for the future. I listened to the Minister of Finance on television on the night of the budget. He was holding a press conference and told the Canadian people that they must pay up today if they want to have oil and gas supplies tomorrow.
That argument is a fraud. There is no guarantee whatsoever that one dollar of the $350 million we are going to collect through the excise tax, or one dollar of the additional $400 million revenue which the oil and gas industry will get, will ever go into exploration for oil or the development of new supplies. Let us look at the experience of the last four years. As I said a few moments ago, the price of oil rose from $2.90 a barrel to $6.50 a barrel and the profits of oil and gas companies in the last four years have broken all previous records. The companies have never done so well.
Don't forget inflation.

Inflation has not risen by over 100 per cent in that period, I point out to the hon. member. The profits of the oil and gas companies of this country are the highest in our history. But what has been the net result in increased exploration
July 22, 1975

and development? Did they spend the extra money they got from the Canadian consumer, with the connivance of the government, on increased exploration? No, they did not. Exploration activity has gone down, not up, for the simple reason that the oil and gas industry held this government up for ransom and said, "We are not going to carry on exploration unless you raise the price still further." That is why the price has risen from $6.50 to $8 per barrel, and why it will rise even more. The pressure continues to be applied to the government. When the government tells us that by giving the oil and gas companies more money we shall be assured of future supplies of gas and oil, its argument is entirely spurious.
We have a shortage now.

As I
said just now, 90 per cent of the production in this country is in the hands of foreign companies, which means that 90 per cent of the profits will go out of Canada. What assurance have we that even one dollar of those profits will come back to Canada to be used in the search for oil or to develop new supplies of oil and gas? There is no assurance at all, unless the government keeps giving the companies more incentives and more hand-outs as it has steadily for the last three or four years.
The other beneficiary of the increase in the price of oil and natural gas is to be the fr.deral treasury. The federal government will collect an extra $450 million from taxing the oil industry and natural gas, in addition to the $350 million it will get from the excise tax of ten cents a gallon which it will use to meet the deficit in the oil compensation payments. Is the government to put any of this $450 million into exploration for oil? On the contrary, it has already announced that it will cut back on the money available for Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada this year will be cut back to $10 million. That is mere bagatelle with which to launch an oil company. No part of the $400 million which the oil and gas industry will get, and no part of the $450 million additional revenue which the federal treasury will get, is earmarked for exploration of development. So when the government tries to tell the people of Canada that they must pay through the nose now in order to be assured of supplies in future, it is misleading the public and deliberately seeking to confuse the consumers of this country.
The second group who are to be the main battlers in the Prime Minister's wrestling match in which inflation is to be wrestled to the ground consists of the workers of this country. They will be called on to pay increased unemployment insurance. When unemployment insurance was originally introduced in this country it was a great step forward. The federal government contributed a fixed percentage of the cost. Later, the federal government par-suaded parliament to amend the legislation in such a way that the federal government was not to contribute anything until unemployment went above 4 per cent. Now the minister has announced that the federal government will not contribute anything until unemployment exceeds a floating eight-year average.

While the business community can pass on this increased tax and increased unemployment insurance payment, this cannot be done by the workers of this country.
I wish to give another illustration. The government intends to use as the shock troops in the fight against inflation the sick, diseased and bedridden of this country. Here the principle is exactly the same. The government calls for sacrifice to cope with inflation, but who is going to suffer? The Minister of Finance announced that the government is giving the required five years' notice to the provinces that they intend to pull out of the hospital insurance plan. He announced that they propose to put a declining ceiling on the increased contribution they will make to medicare. This year medicare costs are anticipated to go up by 16.6 per cent.
