Madam Speaker, I was very interested in listening to the Minister of
July 22, 1975

National Revenue (Mr. Basford) expound this afternoon on what will turn out to be nothing but a witch hunt. I was very disappointed that after the minister made his speech, he left the chamber. I was also interested in the simplicity of the forms he intends to circulate. I have seen a lot of government forms and not many of them have been simple.
I am disappointed in a government which has no faith in the Canadian people. That is exemplified by this government in Bill C-66. I do not dispute the ability of the members of the minister's department, but I think he is giving them a big job. I was also disappointed when the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) asked the minister to table the forms which apply to people eligible for tax refunds and he refused to do so.
This is a government which runs on subsidies and refunds. This is another subsidy they want to hand out, but first they have to take the money from the people. When I was preparing my remarks on this bill it occurred to me that I put a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) concerning the price of gasoline at the retail level. I think it would be interesting to refer to my remarks as reported at page 3664 of Hansard of February 28 of this year. My question was as follows:
In view of the wide discrepancies in the price of gasoline which now varies as much as 14 cents per gallon between service stations for regular gas, will the minister look into this ridiculous situation?
The minister replied:
The government has never attempted to monitor gasoline prices at the retail level. It seems to me that because of the current surplus of products there is extensive competition, at least in some communities, at the retail level. On the whole, I would think that kind of competition would favour the consumer rather than work against him.
Mr. Speaker, I did not ask the minister for a sermon on the merits of competition in the gasoline market. I asked him to look into the situation to see how the industry could sell a product of the same grade at prices which varied as much as 14 cents a gallon, bearing in mind the low margin of profit received by service stations on a gallon of gas. Instead of looking into the matter, what we got from the government was unwarranted interference in the retail sales of gasoline; what we got from the government was taxation by decree instead of by the traditional method of tabling tax bills in the House. To be sure, we are debating the legislation to increase the excise tax, but we are debating it after the fact.
On the night of the budget speech, the operators of gas stations were thrown into a state of chaos. They were not sure whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) could raise the price of gasoline simply by making a statement in the House. They were not sure whether they should raise the price right at that moment. Most service station operators are early risers; they have to open their stations in order to serve other people who need to get an early start. I suppose the average opening time would be about 7 a.m.
The minister said on the night of June 23 that gasoline prices would rise as of that moment by ten cents a gallon.
Excise Tax Act
Surely the minister knows there are mechanical and technical problems involved in the changing of the pricing mechanism on gasoline pumps. It is obvious the minister did not take any of these things into account when he made his announcement. It would appear he placed the burden of responsibility for making the change on the individual operators.
The minister has not explained why the government imposed the tax by decree instead of by tabling legislation and allowing retailers and wholesalers at least a few days in which to prepare themselves for the change. An implementation date of July 1, for instance, would have allowed operators time to dispose of oil inventories and then to impose the increase only on gasoline purchased at the new price.
Apart from the way in which it was done, my chief concern over the price increase is that it will impose a further hardship on tourist operators. My riding of Vic-toria-Haliburton depends to a very large degree on tourism to average out the economic level, and the increase in gasoline prices will not only affect the operating costs of tourist businesses but will also constrict the travel plans of vacationers at a time when we are all trying to encourage Canadians to spend their vacations in their own country; at a time when we are spending millions of dollars on such things as "See Canada First" programs.
Last year, the government imposed a 10 per cent increase in federal taxation on boats and motors, thus posing a threat to the tourist industry and to the power boat and motor industries in this country. After considerable debate, the tax increase on boats was rescinded but the increase in the tax on small motors remained. Now there is a new tax increase on gasoline, with the threat of a further increase next month.
I have to wonder at times whether the government is deliberately trying to scuttle the tourist industry in areas such as I represent. I would be interested to know the amount of real income the government will realize from this tax increase compared with the loss of revenue the tourist operators will suffer. It is no wonder that many people who have spent their working lives in the tourist business are asking whether it is worth the trouble. To a large degree, a tourist operation is a gamble. Just one bad season caused, for instance, by a wet summer, could very well finish off an operation which lacked a strong financial reserve.
There are a number of questions which must be answered with reference to this tax on gasoline. In the first place, it would be interesting to know just how much revenue the government will receive from this tax. According to the latest figures of which I am aware, the amount is likely to be roughly $525 million a year. It should be remembered that merely to collect this amount of extra revenue will cost a good deal of money.
I should also like to mention that the preliminary estimate of the number of those who will be entitled to the gasoline tax refund is between 750,000 and one million. The number of refunds claimed will be considerably greater than the number of eligible refund claimants owing to

July 22, 1975
Excise Tax Act
multiple claims by one claimant during the year. Refunds are expected to total $170 million in this fiscal year, implying a ratio of $1 refunded to every $3 collected.
How is the government going to police this? The Minister of National Revenue made reference to this and said that no bills would be required. We expect Canadians to be honest people, but I think we will have a real witch hunt on our hands here. The Unemployment Insurance Commission is a prime example of what I mean. They have a witch hunt on now, and I am convinced that they are much better equipped to handle it than the Department of National Revenue will be when it comes to collecting this new tax. I think we will have to require bills. I am quite sure in my own mind that bills will be demanded if there is a dispute as to the amount of rebate an individual is claiming. I know this will happen, yet the minister says no bills will be required. I cannot accept that, Madam Speaker.
New section 47 of the act provides for the refund of the gasoline tax to certain types of users of gasoline, such as farmers, commercial fishermen, hunters and federal and provincial agencies. The bill requires those who qualify for the refund to set up accounting procedures, to keep records of gasoline used and the amount of gasoline refund being applied for. This imposes an additional burden upon the users of gasoline. I venture to say the government expects that a great many people will probably not qualify for a large return, and rather than go to the trouble of filling in an application form, simple though the minister says it will be, they will forget about it and file no application. The government is depending on this additional revenue from people who do not trouble to claim a refund. Besides the time and trouble involved, it would also add to the expense of operating a farm or other small business enterprise. The federal bureaucracy is growing so many tentacles that at its present rate of growth it is only a question of time before those tentacles strangle smaller businesses, and only those businesses and industries that are strong enough to absorb this economic punch that is being thrown by the federal government will survive.
As mentioned by previous speakers, I think the government has forgotten the army of commuters travelling to work today. This is a problem, again, due to the lack of adequate housing in areas close to industry. Many of the major arteries into our cities carry large numbers of cars driven by workers commuting back and forth. These people will be penalized, something I do not think the government has taken into consideration. If we had proper accommodation provided for these people in our urban centres, this would relieve our highways of much congestion. But again the government has forgotten about this. Many hundreds of people in the rural riding I represent commute 90 or more miles back and forth to work per day each way.
Returning to my opening statement, the government could have used this opportunity to equalize gasoline prices from one province to another. If the government is so interested in this vital natural resource, why has it not done something to equalize gasoline prices? There must be something wrong. The government has had plenty of time
to do this. One gas station in a given area sells gasoline for 14 cents a gallon less than another sells the same grade: does that not warrant an inquiry? As far as I am concerned, Madam Speaker, it does.
The spread between prices in various regions remains the same, so again I say this tax is simply a means for the government to raise additional revenue. Equalization simply was not in the finance minister's planning when he tabled this legislation, so we will continue to have a wide range of prices for the same product from gas station to gas station, from province to province and from region to region. It is almost as though the government is saying that if we want to live in certain parts of Canada we must be prepared to pay a penalty.
In his budget speech the finance minister wandered all over the lot, and when he did manage to touch base now and again it was to tell us some more bad news. The minister could have used this opportunity to tell the country that the government was prepared to take whatever steps were necessary to see that low interest loans would be made easier for small businesses to obtain. Some of my colleagues have already asked whether the government plans to use the revenue from this tax increase to provide low interest loans to small businesses, such as gasoline service stations. The answer has been given that the government has no intention of using the additional revenue for such purpose. The revenue is going into general revenue to satisfy the government's appetite for more money to spend.
I have received letters and calls from many people in my riding telling me that they cannot get loans to improve their businesses, which the government has been offering at 8 per cent interest. The simple reason is that the banks are not interested in lending money at 8 per cent or 9 per cent when they can get 13 per cent on the same money. There is no way the banks can be forced to lend money to small business operators of the kind I have mentioned, or to anybody else, at low interest rates, so these people end up-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. Again I repeat the remarks I made a while ago. We are dealing with an amendment to Bill C-66, which is to amend the Excise Tax Act.

Thank you very much, Madam Speaker. My reference was to the gasoline industry and to the problems encountered by small business operators. I am also getting complaints from people who tell me that old customers are now pulling up to the pumps at their service station and asking for $2 worth of gasoline, whereas previously they bought a tankful.I know this to be the fact because I have witnessed it myself as well as having had complaints about it. These people say they can buy gas cheaper at stations down the road. As a result, many small, established businesses and filling stations are going to be ruined.
Every community in Canada, large or small, has its service stations, and in many of these smaller communities the service station is the backbone of the town or village economy. In addition to selling gasoline and oil, the service stations keep automobiles, commercial vehicles


and farm vehicles in working order, keeping this business in the local area and contributing to the economic growth of the community. In areas such as my own riding of Victoria-Haliburton they also serve the tourists who come to visit the area.
It has been suggested that the real reason for the increase in the surtax on gasoline is that the government wants to try to conserve petroleum products and that increasing the price is one way to do this. If that is so, then the government is certainly mixed up. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources told me in this House in February that there was a surplus of petroleum products. Everyone knows that you do not get people to stop drinking, smoking or driving simply by increasing the price of cigarettes, alcohol or gasoline. The people who can afford it will still buy gasoline, just as they continue to buy alcohol and cigarettes. It is the people who can least afford the price increase on gasoline who will be hurt, just as they are the ones who are hurt most by any other tax increases.
What will happen to the people who will be forced to spend more money on gasoline? They will ask for more money from their employers. This will add to the inflation. This tax will represent another means by which this government contributes to inflation. This is the government that told us it intended to wrestle inflation to the gound.
I must say that no explanation on the part of the government will satisfy me that there is a justification for this latest increase in the price of gasoline. When one considers that the government estimates it will spend $30 billion in running the country in the coming fiscal year, it certainly seems odd, to say the least, that it requires the paltry $300 million to $525 million that will be raised by means of this tax. I say "paltry" because it seems this government considers any sum under $1 billion to be paltry.
There is a story that has gone the rounds for years concerning the mountain climber who was asked why he climbed the mountain. He replied that he climbed it because it was there. I am wondering whether the Minister of Finance decided to place a tax on gasoline on June 23 simply because it was there. When the minister has finished clearing up the mess in respect of collecting refunds in relation to this gasoline tax, I think he will wish he had looked elsewhere for additional revenue. Now we have been told by the Minister of National Revenue that the government will tax the refund in respect of commercial users of gasoline. Here we have another example of the government contributing to the costs of individuals.
Now I should like to deal with the record of the government in handling the oil situation. In the winter of 1973-74 the government created what I believe was an artificial crisis in respect of fuel oil. We were told by the minister that there was a huge shortage of fuel oil. There was no shortage, but the price of home heating oil was increased. We see from Hansard for April 2, 1974, that the government paid 991/2 cents per gallon for Rumanian oil while the world market price for oil was only 89 cents. Later, in Hansard for April 11, 1974, we note that the quality of the oil was so poor that the government received offers for it of 15 cents a gallon.
Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I fail to see the relevance of the hon. member's comments to the amendment or the bill under discussion. Perhaps the hon. member would limit his remarks to the bill.

With all respect, Madam Speaker, may I say we are still dealing with the oil situation. However, I shall move on. The gas tax and increases in the cost of home heating oil will generate revenue of about $2 billion. Once again, however, this amount will not go to the government for the purpose of expanding supply. This $2 billion in national revenue will certainly make up for the elimination of the 5 per cent tax on insulation building materials. I stress "insulation building materials". Back in 1974, as a party we advocated the dropping of the 11 per cent tax on building materials. The government gradually climbed down the ladder; it reduced the tax from 11 per cent to 5 per cent. Now the 5 per cent has been eliminated in respect of insulation materials. I do not know why the government did not go all the way and drop the 5 per cent tax on all building materials.
That would be too sensible.

That is right, it would be too sensible. This blatant tax grab will have severe repercussions in the province of Ontario. It is estimated that the increase in the cost of fuel alone in Ontario will eliminate 15,000 jobs. It will certainly hit very hard the auto industry in Ontario. There is no emergency at present that would justify the undermining of the livelihood of as many citizens as will be the case in respect of this bill.
In closing may I say that because of the representations made by many members of this House, chiefly opposition members and a few members on the government side, in respect of this unwarranted tax and the effect it will have on the Canadian economy, I hope the minister will review the situation and withdraw this bill.

Madam Speaker, if there was any question about a silly season in Ottawa, I think it is quite evident it has arrived. The proof of it is clear. Even as I rise now, speaking on the government side as a backbencher, there will be those who will say I am prolonging the debate. Last night the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie), speaking on the other side, complained that no Liberals had spoken in the debate on that day. We on this side are damned if we speak to defend the measure before us and we are damned if we do not rise.
I say it is a silly season. All members know that the weather gets warm in Ottawa in July and August. The hotter it gets, the more perverse hon. members become. Each side says publicly it does not mind sitting, while privately it says something else. As a local MP it is easier for me to come here than it is for some others. Some hon. members, however, seem to treat these sittings as a form of penance for having received a salary increase recently.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I regret interrupting the hon. gentleman but I should remind him that we are dealing with Bill C-66. Would the hon. member confine his remarks to the bill.

July 22, 1975
Excise Tax Act

Madam Speaker, I think my remarks are relevant to the bill. Few hon. members opposite have reached the point of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), the House leader for the official opposition, who is quoted in this morning's Globe and Mail as saying that the government has been tampering with the air conditioning system to bring the opposition to its knees. I have a direct quotation from the Globe and Mail of this morning in which it is stated that the hon. member charged that the government has resorted to this measure to try to bring an end to the debate on Bill C-66. I cannot suggest a more direct proof of the silly season.
Every conceivable point that could be made in this debate has been made many times over. From previous experience, I look over to the other side of the House and wonder when the vote will come. It could not have come last night because there were not enough MPs present on the other side. Today it looks better. If a vote does not come soon, then we will see a corporal's guard do duty for each party and nothing will pass the House. I remember the summer of 1964 when we sat all summer on the flag debate. Eventually it was terminated by closure. Hon. members may well ask: Why are we here? Surely at this stage no one will be persuaded by reasonable arguments to change his or her vote.
Why does this charade go on? All hon. members are in favour of a one price system for petroleum products, with allowances for local transportation costs across Canada. In order to find the extra $350 million needed to subsidize foreign crude oil imported into eastern Canada, the government has proposed a tax of ten cents per gallon on gasoline, with rebates for commercial and industrial users.
No one likes a tax, and it is a great thing for the voters back home to fight taxes. Some say that the government should have made savings in other programs, without specifying where, or else that a program such as that carried out by Information Canada be abolished, which would by no means provide the sums of money needed.
Others say the subsidy should be financed out of general revenues. This is a good problem for economic theorists: comparison of the merits of a user tax versus a combination of personal and corporate income taxes. I am by no means satisfied that non-automobile owners, frequently elderly and retired, should be taxed to pay the import subsidy on gasoline. On the other hand, we all recognize that many people who have no choice but to travel to and from work by private automobile are hurt by the ten cents per gallon tax. But, as I said, it is a debate that the academic theorists can go into until the end of time.
Unfortunately, there is no perfect tax. The present measure appears, in my view, to be as good, as practical, and as fair as any that can be proposed in the present circumstances.
Oh, oh!

I hear interruptions from hon. members opposite in the NDP. They have their own whipping boy. It is all the fault of the multinational oil corporations. I am not prepared to say that these corporations may not have taken advantage of the situation to improve their
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
profits. That is possible. But last night in this House the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) cited the profits of Imperial Oil and said they were on strike, not doing exploration for new oil. When I pointed out that Imperial Oil has the largest exploration budget in the Mackenzie delta in its history, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) shouted "Yes, but they are spending our money". The logic of these arguments escapes me.
One thing is clear; the NDP has a new leader, or is it the same old one? And they must make a noise. They have taken the old drum, put a new coat of paint on it, and are beating it hard. The new-old leader announced on radio that he would keep the House here all summer on the Unemployment Insurance Act changes. Since the government did not oblige him by calling this measure for debate, his group have since been trying to make all the political capital they can out of opposing gasoline taxes.
The real opposition to the excise tax on gasoline comes from the official opposition, the Conservative Party. As everyone knows, this party really has no policy on the petroleum issue. In western Canada they rally round the Premier of Alberta, Mr. Lougheed, and demand that the so-and-so easterners pay more for western energy. In eastern Canada they bleat for the consumers, echoing Premier Bill Davis of Ontario. By opposing this special tax they can agree on something, and hide the differences in their ranks.
The real difficulty, Mr. Speaker-and, I suggest, the clue to this debate-is to be found in the fact that an election is to be called in Ontario very soon. After groping for an issue, and finding none, Bill Davis consulted his opinion polls. Last spring they told him that he was not doing so well.
Now Bill Davis has found what he hopes will be his fighting ground. He is going to campaign, it seems, against the federal budget. He will help the North American automobile industry, and will stimulate more housing activity. Finally, he proposes to be a great friend of the gas-buying car driver by a program that will delay still further any increase in gas prices due to raising the price of crude oil.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) had increased the basic price of western Canadian crude oil from $6.50 to $8 per barrel effective July 1, equivalent to five cents per gallon retail. Because of existing stocks many refineries stood to make windfall profits if they had been allowed to increase their prices immediately. They were asked to delay price increases for 45 days; this is until August 15. Premier Bill Davis went one better; he extended the freeze for 90 days-that is until September 30.
Hear, hear!

I hear hon. members applauding, including my friend from eastern Ontario. But we in eastern Ontario are most apprehensive about what will happen to us in the period between August 15 and September 30. Our gasoline comes from Montreal refineries using imported crude. As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) pointed out, Montreal refineries, on the average, have smaller stocks of refined products than the refineries serving Toronto, based on western Canadian crude. Ninety days may not work as much of a hardship for the large
July 22, 1975

Toronto refineries, but many Montreal refineries will be using $8 per barrel oil long before Bill Davis' 90 days are up.
What will happen then? Will these Montreal refineries refuse to ship refined gasoline to eastern Ontario, including Ottawa? Will there be line-ups at the gas pumps? Or will Dr. Claude Isbister, an economist newly appointed to look into these matters by the government of Ontario, persuade Bill Davis that eastern Ontario gas prices will have to follow the same pattern as prices in Montreal? In that case Ontario will have its own two price system for gasoline for 45 days-a lower price for Toronto, and a higher one for eastern Ontario. But, as they say, Toronto is where the provincial action is. At this stage I confidently predict a provincial election to be called in Ontario, to be held before September 30. Eastern Ontario will not really count when the time comes.
Tell us how it will come out.

I do not have the capability of predicting the future. I have learned from my own previous experience, and I am a little timid about making predictions. I would simply say that I am confident voters in Ontario will come up with the right choice.
I appeal to hon. members from all opposition parties to put an end to the silly season in the House of Commons. Let Bill C-66 and the amendments come to a vote. There is really no further political capital to be made in prolonging this.debate.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I am quite pleased to take part in this debate. I know that several members are asking questions, given the length of the debate, but we believe on this side of the House that it is our duty to refute and fight that legislation which will su?ely sorely try a certain group of people, namely the workers. This is why we cannot accept such a legislation compelling a very special group, that is the low income group, to attain the objective of this budget-essential according to the government-which amounts to $500 million a year.
I heard a few minutes ago the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) coming up with fancy ideas and suggesting that the three parties of the opposition could be blamed for the delayed refunds, because the bill not being passed, the Department of National Revenue is unable to make the necessary refunds. It would perhaps have been advisable to vote that legislation before enforcing it. Then there would have been no delayed refund.
If we really wanted to examine the difficulties that this bill will bring to a very particular class of people that the workers are, it might not be necessary to make refunds because I felt, and I still do, that it might have been possible to recover that money that seems to be necessary to reach the objective of a single price across Canada, perhaps through income tax.
Excise Tax Act
We are wondering seriously. Why those exemptions? Why those exemptions for certain classes of people who can afford a lot more to pay than the working class? I will limit myself once again in this debate to reflecting the sufferings and difficulties caused to that working class that cannot get out of it otherwise. Exemptions are awarded to certain classes that are certainly in better position to meet the objective of the government that seems necessary-the budget-but that lets the workers support this weight.
I heard several members and I read over several speeches. In our ridings, Madam Speaker, all members, government members as well as opposition members, witnessed scores of representations made by voters who plead with the members of every riding to make the government see reason on this legislation that we regard as discriminatory and unfair. We regard it as such and we believe we are right. We know quite well that it is the same thing for government members, Madam Speaker. We know the system. There is no mistake about it. So should we defend the minister even if he is wrong? But in the circumstances we are being accused of delaying this debate. However, I would like it to be said out loud. We think we are discharging a responsability we have in this House of not supporting a legislation when it is bad. Of course, the system often leads us-on both sides of the House-to exaggerate on certain measures. But on Bill C-66 which provides for the increase and the recovery of $500 million a year to be paid by a class of workers who have no chance of getting out of it, we are going to fight that legislation, Madam Speaker, and I think we are right in doing so.
Last week I listened to the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) when she said she was courageous enough to implement an unpopular measure. An income tax increase is always unpopular, but I think it is more fairly distributed than the legislation now before us.
But if we go back to the eve of the election a year ago, it is clear that no one would have dared introduce such a measure, and today, considering the good mood in which the government seemed to be a year ago, such measures are proposed. This afternoon, I pointed out to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) a decision of his department that is hurting a group of dairy producers which had been promised a fair return. But through another measure the left hand takes away what the right hand had given them. Similarly, it is said with haste that taxes were not raised in the new budget. But in an oblique way, workers have their pockets picked of a tax nothing but direct.
And as far as we are concerned, we believe our duty is to fight a legislation that appears to be most unfair. For these reasons, we will go on urging the government to show more concern, more perception, and of course more fairness to all Canadians.
We have no contention with the single price of gasoline throughout Canada, out we cannot accept the way in which the money is to be picked in one group's pockets.
As was stated earlier by one of my colleagues, such a measure goes a long way toward antagonizing both the provinces and the tourist industry already burdened by inflation. Clearly, such a measure is most harmful to

July 22, 1975
Excise Tax Act
tourist operators. It has also been suggested by another member that normally gasoline taxes are imposed by provinces to the extent needed for the construction of highways.
These provinces are antagonized once more. The government might say: Let provinces impose additional taxes. But we know perfectly well that there is a limit to that, and with this very heavy burden the provinces will be reluctant to seek the extra money needed to improve highways. We have there another negative effect of this legislation. We are trying to draw the government's attention to the shortcomings of this bill, the difficulties in implementing it, and it is our responsibility to remind the government of its own responsibilities.
It is not for the fun of it that we have been discussing this legislation for something like 10 days. And if it means discussing it 10 more days, I believe our responsibility is to do so, as recommended by our constituents.
How many of our constituents, as of today, have been asking us not to pass the bill, to make every effort to stop it. Some hon. members apparently think this is amusing. They should first explain it in their constituencies. How is it possible to suggest that people are against it in my constituency, but in the next one people favour such an increase?
Naturally, the minister spoke of that redistribution, of levying that unfair tax, and also of the categories that will be exempted. If he will give us the assurance that all the workers who have to use their cars to get to work will also be exempted, I think we could then make a compromise fairly quickly. Let him make us that proposal. Then, to my mind, we will not have pleaded for a bad cause, but will have won over the government to a far more humane bill, because the bill now strikes us as being unacceptable, and of course most unfair.
Under the circumstances, we must therefore continue to ask the government to lend us an attentive ear.
It is hard to understand, considering all the difficulties we have had in the last few years, the effects of a budget which was intended to be anti-inflationary when in fact it will be anything but. Even now, everyone recognizes that it will result in an increase in the cost of living. Yet, the budget was introduced as a measure to check inflation. This bill will achieve exactly the opposite. We therefore fail to understand the position of the government and its refusal to come back to its senses and redistribute the levy required to achieve its objective, but leaving out of it the poor worker, who has been tortured enough in the last few years, and who will now know greater difficulties because of a bill no one would have dared introduce on the eve of an election, which everyone knows. But the government has a majority, and elections will be held in four years.
They could not care less about the difficulties the bill will create. Of course, we will be blamed for prolonging the debate, because we have enough conscience to want to reply. Because we insist on doing so, we choose to oppose this bill. A few government members rose and tries to justify the actions of their government. We understand this system, but I do not believe, Madam Speaker, anyone

can be truly honest in letting the burden of that legislation fall on the shoulders of that group of workers instead of applying it in a much more equitable way.
Madam Speaker, when the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) talked earlier, it was clear to anyone who can read between the lines that he wanted to let the public know that refunds might be delayed because the opposition is objecting to that measure. But we repeat he can keep those refunds, because as far as I am concerned, Madam Speaker, we shall object for quite a long time to that legislation which we consider unfair. And I think it is the duty of the opposition to oppose the government which introduces such an unfair and unacceptable measure which discriminates against a particular group of citizens. I dare hope we will object to that measure until the government will water its wine and consider a more equal distribution. Madam Speaker, we only want that money to be distributed and collected if necessary. And we think it is necessary, there is no doubt about that. We have the same ends as the government, but not the same means. And that is the important point.
As I said earlier, I read again several speeches. How come that after so many speeches have been made, after so many members got information in their constituencies and were made aware of the difficulties their constituents were faced with, we are the only ones on this side of the House who believe this legislation to be a bad one? It is unthinkable! Any honest minded person, Madam Speaker, will agree with the good arguments which were put forward on this side of the House. And there are good, true arguments, and the public is asking for and demanding a very strong stand against such a discriminatory legislation, as I said earlier.
Therefore, it is not by letting the Canadian people believe that we are going to delay the refunds that we will increase our credibility. I repeat that, truly and honestly, this legislation should not have been applied before it was passed and the debate over. This fierce battle that we are waging against this legislation could certainly have been prevented, had the government assumed its responsibilities and applied this legislation only after it was duly adopted. The government wanted to apply it before it was adopted, and it will not be long before it accuses us of delaying payment of refunds. I do not believe that this argument weighs much against ours, Madam Speaker. I feel that we are meeting the wishes of a group of people who had enough difficulties as it was without having to face new ones, and it is in the interest of the workers who need to use their cars daily. Some hon. members have indeed referred to public transportation in a number of larger communities. Maybe adequate public transportation does exist, but we are all perfectly aware that public transportation services are inadequate in thousands of municipalities where workers must cover long distances to get to work.
Therefore, the argument of the Minister of Finance inviting the public to use public transport will not be valid as long as the government has not done more to better organize these services. The public is therefore invited to use a tool which does not exist in several areas. We find these arguments very weak and not applicable to the potential of an area or a society who needs them.
July 22, 1975

The government should not repeat that it has the courage to apply an unpopular measure. Through the income tax, it could have decreed a certain increase which would not have been popular, but would have been much fairer than making a certain category of people pay the price of this policy. It is with this in mind that we shall continue to ask the government to better understand the difficulties that this will cause for workers and that we shall try to make the government understand that our interventions are motivated by the requests of our constituents. Indeed, I am convinced that constituents of the government members have already shown their concern and asked their representatives in Parliament to urge the minister to propose a better distribution as concerns his objectives. In view of the circumstances, we believe that we are doing our duty even if certain government members are under the impression that we are delaying the proceedings of the House on purpose. I do not believe that we are delaying unduly the debates, but this gives us an opportunity to repeat, as we must, that the government does not seem to understand that this measure is unfair and discriminatory. We cannot repeat this too much.
Is the hon. member leaving us for the provincial government?

And I want the population to know that the opposition is doing its duty in this debate and that it will do so conscienciously. I also invite Montreal members, and those from other areas, to speak up. If there is agreement about the fact that the worker must be the only one to bear the burden of this legislation, let us say so and let us remember-
Will the hon. member speak a little louder?
We do not agree-
You will make the headlines.

-with the fact that the government should apply such a measure.
Maybe hon. members should rise more often. If they are tired of headlines, they will surely not have the best headlines by remaining silent as they now do and by supporting their ministers with a silence that proves to be intellectually dishonest. I, as well as the population, deplore such silence. For us, on this side of the House, this is no pleasurable experience, I am sorry to say, because I regret still being here in this House fighting such a piece of legislation, and all my colleagues would like, as is the case for many members, to end this session on a pleasant note. We have to bear this responsibility, we have commitments, and we would be making a serious mistake if we were to leave the government pass so bad a piece of legislation in such an easy way. And the population would blame us. Nevertheless, the legislation will pass.
Is the hon. member leaving for his holidays?

We want the population to be witness to this discriminatory measure on the part of a government which casts aside the interests and problems of a part of our working population. That is our goal. I feel that we are thus carrying out our responsibilities as members of Parliament. Members opposite us have also made commitments during the last election campaign, when they prom-
Excise Tax Act
ised a just society. We are still a long way from such a society. Simply have a look at our legislation, such as the bill on unemployment insurance which is still more unjust that the one before us now. Rest assured, that one is far from being passed. We have a part to play, we are going to play it, and from now on we are going to play it with regard to measures that prove harmful to our society, and it will be no fun. I wish to reassure my colleagues sitting opposite. We will not let such bad and unjust laws get through Parliament. From now on, we will do our utmost to make the population aware of such a bad piece of legislation and of the government's lack of sincerity.
Petty politics!
Is the hon. member leaving tonight? Happy holidays!

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock tonight.
At 6 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.
Question.

Mr. Speaker, I am extremely pleased this evening to discuss Bill C-66 meant to enforce some budgetary proposals which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) presented to the House on June 23 last and especially those concerning amendments to the excise tax.
I remember well, Mr. Speaker, that during his budget speech the Minister of Finance stated concerning the 10c. tax on gas that he wanted in the first place to finance the subsidy which would enable to maintain a flat price for oil throughout Canada and thus promote the conservation of energy. I admit that the government must take some steps to find additional funds to subsidize oil but to compel once again the average wage earner to foot the bill, this is something else! I entirely disagree with the Minister of Finance on that point.
There is no doubt that through this bill, the government is trying, by every possible means, to increase its revenue, but it is extremely deplorable that once again the average wage earner, particularly, is footing the bill. In mentioning that, I think immediately of the person who uses his car to get to work and earn his family's keep. The car is not a luxury to him, but a real necessity. He will have to buy gas, regardless of its cost.
Mr. Speaker, the 10-cent tax a gallon of gas will net the government something like $525 million but, on the other hand, that unjust tax will do much harm to some people, specially those on low income. Once again, the lowwage earner will be hardest hit by that increase in the cost of gas. Indeed, those people realize easily that it is costing ever more to earn enough to give their families a decent living, for the low wage earner lacks purchasing power.

July 22, 1975
Excise Tax Act
In my view, Mr. Speaker, the tax on gasoline will simply contribute to fan inflation more and more, and I sincerely believe that the government is taxing people who cannot afford this increase, for there is no doubt the federal government will get the $525 million revenue which this tax will bring, out of the pockets of low income people. It could easily have raised the money by taxing the big, multinational corporations, thus redistributing Canadian wealth in a non-discriminatory way among Canadians.
Under the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government compels motorists to use public transportation. As my colleague from Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) said yesterday, and I share his view, people would use public transport if they were available to them.
As I have said, when it comes to encouraging people to use public transport, one must bear in mind that many workers such as those in my constituency have to travel 20, 30 and 50 miles to work, and have to use their private cars to drive to specific places.
As a result of this increase, they are particularly penalized. As for the argument that the increase would favour the saving of unrenewable energy, I do not feel it would have that much of an impact because I consider that the government is taxing only one part of energy users instead of truly tackling the energy problem.
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is hoping that fewer people will be using their cars for leisure. Honestly, I am clearly under the impression that those who use their cars simply for leisure are going to keep on purchasing gas no matter what the price, and any piece of legislation aiming at saving gas, such as this one, will have no effect on those people.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it is surely not a step in the right direction, because this increase will not discourage people from using the family car on weekends. One must realize that a person who takes his car to work in the morning does not really have any other means of transportation; it is more economical for him or public means of transportation, as I said earlier, are not flexible enough or have inconvenient schedules.
In reality, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government is simply falling back on small wage earners and is also discriminating against the consumers who are the mainstay of our society. Moreover, those who will not pay the surtax will be able over and above that to deduct from their income their car expenses for business purposes. Whereas the small wage earner who will have to take the urban transit system to go to work during the week and who will want some time during the weekend to drive his wife and children out of the big city to be able to breathe something else than polluted air for some days will have to pay this surtax.
Following this way of thinking, one could suggest that the merchant who decides to go and watch a baseball or football game during his working hours will be able to charge his gas expenses to the advertising account of his company and this way he will abstain from paying this surtax.

Mr. Speaker, it is very unfortunate but in fact, I cannot see any meaning in this, and I consider that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) will certainly never reach his two targets, namely .to finance the grants maintaining a single oil price across Canada and to encourage the conservation of energy, as I said at the very beginning of my speech. This increase only aggravates the economic situation which is already unsound. Finally, Mr. Speaker, it is only an inflationary, an unconsidered move, as so many other moves made by this government over the past years. Therefore I am forced to vote against this bill which only aggravates the situation of low income people which is already difficult.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, when considering the budget, the minister should have set a higher tax on alcohol and on tobacco instead of saddling low income earners with a tax on gasoline. Maybe the Minister of Finance does not know that many people need their car to earn a living. But the government preferred to ignore the people. If it had, of course profits would have been considerably smaller than they will be with the excise tax on gasoline. Maybe the minister and the government think that in three years, when the new election will take place, people will have forgotten that budget, but I personally do not believe such a blow below the belt can be easily forgotten.
When I meet people in my constituency, they ask me questions like this one: Does the government ever think of us? And among those people, there are gas station managers who frequently ask me the same question. Big companies increased the price of gasoline. Today, the government is helping them increase it again, and adds to that increase through a tax. Once again, big companies will drive considerable benefits. And we shall pay for it all, since the salaries of pump attendants will have to be increased. Mr. Speaker, in all this, gas station managers have never had the opportunity to increase their profits at the same rate as the salaries they have to pay their employees now.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand how the government could wrestle inflation if they go on increasing prices every year, and I am no economist, but I think it is ridiculous to add fuel to inflation in such a way.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I plead with all my colleagues in this House, since the present government has a majority, to put an end to that discussion, and to all those speeches which all sound alike and are of no avail to the people. Since June 24, people have been paying a 10 cent tax on gasoline, while the bill has not yet been passed; and if my hon. colleagues decide to put an end to that debate, we in this House will all have an opportunity to spend a few days with our families and especially with our children who otherwise will have to go back to school in some time without having taken the full benefit of holidays with their whole family. I hear my colleagues from the government applauding me. I thank them for it. But if ever speeches do not stop, I shall once again ask those who have just applauded, I shall ask them to urge the Minister of Finance to withdraw the bill so that we can all take holidays.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak about a large number of people in my riding on whom the ten cents a gallon excise tax on gasoline places a very great burden. I speak of the many people who work in Fredericton and who must drive to and from their work because there is for them no alternative mode of transportation.
The city of Fredericton has taken over the public bus transportation system which operates only within the city limits. Although many people use this form of transportation, others find that it does not meet their needs. For those who live outside the city there is no form of regular public transportation which can take people to and from their work. The cost of land in the city of Fredericton and the scarcity of it in recent years make it prohibitive for average citizens to buy a building lot and so they must move outside the city to find a building lot they can afford.
What of the farmers in Millville, the workers in the St. Anne-Nackawic Mill, and the folks in Temperancevale who must travel to Fredericton for medical treatment? How else can they get there except by car?
People who live in communities like Stanley, McGivney, Durham, Bloomfield, New Maryland, Keswick and Zealand go to Fredericton to trade. How? There is only one way-by motor vehicle. There is no luxury. It is essential service.
People living in the Fredericton area travel to Oromocto to work, and vice-versa. Some are able to travel by bus; most are not. Civil servants, military personnel, hospital workers, some travel by bus, most cannot. They travel by motor car. There is no other way.
Senior citizens on fixed incomes who get a little pleasure from travelling around the beautiful landscape in central New Brunswick during our lovely maritime summer will find that their little pleasure is also taxed, and it is apparently the government's policy to restrict pleasure driving for senior citizens who have certainly earned the right to avail themselves of this form of recreation. The many wonderful people who on Sunday afternoons take shut-ins out for a drive through the lovely rolling hills in the New Brunswick countryside are also going to be penalized by this tax.
One of New Brunswick's most outstanding industries is the tourist industry and the selection of July 1 as the date when this new tax would be imposed on motor vehicle operators could not have been selected with greater skill if its intention were to hit our tourist industry at the time when it would hurt us most. For our woods workers and farmers, the trip to Fredericton on Friday night or Saturday afternoon to do their shopping, and the trip for a large and growing number of citizens to Saturday morning market in Fredericton are essential for the procurement of food and clothing. For most of these people there is no alternative public transportation system. They must travel in their motor car. Now it is going to cost a lot more and they can ill afford the increase.
These are the Canadians who carry the brunt of the tax. Che tax is not a deterrent to them to use less energy

I submit that a one price system and any subsidy in connection with it should be supported from the general revenues of this country. In my opinion a ten cents a gallon tax on gasoline is the poorest type of tax which could be imposed. Without question, the government must increase its revenues to support a one price system, but to do so by imposing hardship on the people who can least afford to bear it does not appear to me to be an exercise in wisdom.
If my calculations are correct, the increase in the government's revenues as a consequence of the ten cents a gallon increase on gasoline, the increase by $1.50 a barrel in the price of crude oil and the 43 cents per thousand cubic feet increase in the price of natural gas will exceed by at least twice the revenue required to cover the difference between the payment to the eastern provinces and the revenue from the export subsidy levied by the Government of Canada on oil exports.
I hope the minister will reconsider his decision in regard to the ten cents excise tax on gas and consider the discriminatory aspect of it. I suggest that this does virtually nothing for conservation and it is not appropriate for funding the one price policy.
We, in my party, consider the tax to be intolerable because it falls mainly on the working people. In my view the subsidization of the one price system should be a general charge against the national treasury and not against the motorist.

If the government is serious in its desire to conserve petroleum and reduce our dependence on imported foreign oil for a high percentage of our energy needs, I suggest that we focus our most serious attention on one of the greatest energy potentials in the world which can free millions of barrels of oil every year, and year after year.
At the head of the Bay of Fundy between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia we have one of the most tremendous energy potentials in the world in the form of tidal power. The tides rise and fall some 50 feet twice a day, day in and day out, and this phenomenon will go on forever into the future. The magnitude of this tidal range is higher than anywhere else in the world. The volume of water which regularly and predictably rushes into this unique funnel shaped topography between our two provinces amounts to many times the flow of water in the Saint Lawrence River. The energy which this volume of water could generate when passing through turbines amounts to billions of kilowatt hours when converted into electric energy, and in turn represents millions of barrels of oil available every year, and year after year.
The feasibility of tidal power development in the Bay of Fundy was studied and reported upon in 1969. A review of this study was reported in this House during this session of parliament, and that review recommended five phased studies to move the project forward. These studies are not progressing with the dynamic energy that the current energy crisis requires. It would seem to me that a crash program financed and spearheaded by the Government of Canada is essential if Canada is to meet its energy needs in the immediate future and by the end of the century.
Another area worthy of immediate study by a government seeking to reduce energy consumption is a straight line highway, a direct route from New Brunswick to central Canada through the State of Maine, the Corridor Road, a route that could cut hundreds of miles off the travel distance between central and Atlantic Canada, and for commercial traffic this means hundreds of miles each week and thousand of gallons of gasoline each year.
I would also suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has stated, this is an energy conservation measure, the government give full consideration to allowing motorists to deduct from their taxable income-the cost of engine tune ups, carburetor cleanings, air filters, and any other repairs to their vehicles which would increase gasoline mileage and reduce air pollution. This would offer some assistance to the motorists who wish to help the Minister of Finance conserve energy without being punished financially for their good intentions.
My suggestion is that the answer to the problem is not in taxing poor people for whom motor car transportation is essential, but lies in a form of positive leadership in developing alternative sources of energy and supporting the one price system out of the general revenues of our country where the criterion for raising the money should be the ability to pay and not a discriminatory tax like this which hits the hardest those least able to pay.

This tax again underlines the failure of the government to give leadership and focus the attention of all departments of government on the matter of regional disparity in the maritimes. DREE invests funds in transportation policies, or the lack of them, and then erodes industrial potential. The Treasury Board pays workers at lower regional rates, and now the Department of Finance exposes workers to severe hardship.
There is no strategy; there is no over-all plan; there is no determination to exterminate regional disparity. But there is a challenge and this government, or more likely the one that succeeds it, must accept the call of the Canadian people to get into the arena and win the day for them. So be it.

Mr. Speaker, in rising in this debate on Bill C-66 I am concerned about a number of things. The bill deals with four topics. If we quickly move from air transportation it strikes me that at first blush this bill is designed to encourage people to stay home, don't drive, but get drunk.
It appears that this bill encourages people to stay home because they will be taxed ten cents a gallon if they get out their cars and drive. Obviously they will remain in their homes because the government has been generous enough to take the tax off insulation materials, which will represent a saving of about $25 per house, and has taken the tax off wine.
I could not help but be somewhat amused by the comments of the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) who spoke in this debate the other night. Since this amendment seeks to delay this bill for a period of six months the hon. member seemed to suggest our attitude was that we should not do anything to solve the problem, that we should just stick our heads in the sand for six months and maybe it would go away. She said this is a terrible thing, that it is an ostrich-like attitude. She said that her government is providing outstanding leadership.
It was very funny when the next day the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) did not try to hoist something for six months but tried to hoist the PLO and the crime conference for an indefinite period. I can only hope that maybe he will stick his head in sand for an indefinite period.
The most obvious function of the excise tax bill is cruelly to put in place an onerous tax of ten cents a gallon on the working poor. I am not sure that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) introduced the measure in the budget on June 23 he really knew what he was doing. On June 23 the minister said this was a conservation measure. On June 25 he said he had not carried out any study to determine how much gasoline would be conserved. He hoped it would be a conservation measure but said that really it was to raise revenue, some $350 million this year, and a larger sum in a full fiscal year.
When asked how the rebates would work and how the people would apply, the Minister of Finance at that time said that they did not have the regulations yet, that he was not too sure but that he hoped the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) would detail these regulations during the budget debate. During the budget debate the Minister of National Revenue had nothing to say, and we

He said yes, there would be rebates. As a matter of fact he said the government could implement a rebate system within two to three weeks. Then he added "We don't plan on issuing any rebates until after Labour Day". So it appears that if the bill passes this week, although there would be almost six weeks to Labour Day, he does not intend to implement rebates within two to three weeks, as he said he could; the government is going to wait until after Labour Day. I can only come to the conclusion that his statement about implementing them within two to three weeks is hogwash.
The minister did not throw much light on the regulations. He said people would have to fill out a form and would have to send the form in to claim a rebate. If a person was owed as much as $200 a month rebate, then he could apply monthly. However, if a rebate were anything less than $200, a person would have to apply semi-annually.
If a person, for example, was owed $150 a month, this means that at the end of a six month period he would have $900 owed him by the government. This does not strike me as very equitable and it draws a distinction between large users, which will likely be the big corporations, and the small users of gasoline, say an independent salesman. The government is forgetting the small, independent businessman, the small contractor or industry. They will have to borrow this $900 from the bank. If they are on an overdraft, they might have to pay 11 to 13 per cent interest, and, as I say, the situation does not strike me as at all equitable.
The minister said that the forms people will have to fill in have been drafted, but when we asked him to table one of these forms, he said he could not. I can only conclude that he does not have any forms to table. Indeed, I do not think the government in fact knows what it is doing. If I may use an expression of the Liberals and return it to them, they are asking the people to buy a pig in a poke. We have the pig all right, and would like to find out what the government intends to do with it.

The fact is that this ten cents a gallon excise tax is a very regressive tax. If I may fairly state the matter, when the government is under attack for bringing in an unfair tax it should have the decency, if it intends to represent the people of this country, to reconsider its position. Obviously the Liberals seem to be digging in their heels. The Minister of Finance does not appear here to listen to the debate; he is represented by his parliamentary secretary, who himself is not listening but talking to another member. The government does not really know what is going on. Hon. members opposite have not been out on the hustings to question people up and down the streets of the cities of this country.
I do not mean to be antagonistic to my hon. friends opposite who presently form the government, but let me compare this with another situation where a government imposed a very unpopular and, if I may say so, regressive tax. Some two or three years ago the Honourable John White, then treasurer of the government of Ontario, introduced a 7 per cent tax on heating oil. This was a regressive tax which was attacked by all parties, including his own. The Conservative party, the government of Ontario, and the treasury had enough guts to say, "We have been wrong, it is a regressive measure", and the treasurer withdrew it. We do not find this happening with the arrogant people on the other side who merely want to rip off the Canadian public to line the treasury of the federal government, at the same time trying to hide behind energy conservation.
This regressive tax measure will cost the average working person some $200 to $300 a year out of his or her after tax income, taking into account increased heating fuel costs and unemployment insurance premiums as well. Surely by taking that much out of the taxpayers' after tax income the government is not only fuelling inflation but is encouraging inflation by inviting another round of increased wage demands.
It should be pointed out that price increases exert a direct and measurable upward pressure on costs, and a direct and measurable downward pressure on job creation. They are inflationary, increase unemployment and can erode our industrial competitiveness in many ways. For example, since funds will be taken out of people's pockets they will not be able to buy the goods that manufacturers put on the market.
It strikes me that these negative effects do not bear equally on all Canadians. This is obvious in terms of the worker who finds himself unable to secure a job. According to a recent United States study reported in the energy policy project of the Ford Foundation, families with an annual income of less than $2,500 spent 15.2 per cent of their income to purchase energy, whereas those with an income exceeding $24,500 spent 4.1 per cent. A University of Toronto study indicated exactly the same position in Canada. It is only fair to point out that because of this tax poor people will have to spend a disproportionate amount of their income on energy compared to rich people.
Oil and gas price escalation is a regressive form of taxation that will contribute to inflation and unemployment, as well as to the dislocation of the economy. At such

time when inflation is contained and unemployment in Canada is substantially reduced, it may be appropriate to consider higher prices of fuel, but not in the manner of this ten cents a gallon excise tax. I believe the federal proposal announced in the budget is an unreasonable one. Along with the increase in home heating costs it will generate some $2 billion in additional revenue. But it will not provide extra money to the companies to enable them to find new oil. The proceeds of the tax go directly to Ottawa. I believe, moreover, that its imposition will have severe repercussions in the province of Ontario. In the next 12 months we shall see the consumer price index rising by 2 per cent because of these increases in fuel prices. Then, because of the loss of purchasing power in the hands of consumers, we shall find there are upward of 15,000 fewer jobs in the province.
To say this tax will damage industry is to put it mildly. Already, throughout Ontario and in other parts of the country as well, resort and tourist operators are suffering. People are not bringing their boats from the United States into the Rideau Canal system or into the Trent and Severn systems because they can use their boats more cheaply at home. The minister brought this tax in just as an important industry was getting off the ground, and it is having an unfortunate effect on employment in this area.
The minister estimates this ten cents tax will generate some $350 million but he does not tell us how much it will cost to administer. I suggest that a healthy proportion of the money will be eaten up by administrative costs. And while the government keeps the money, individuals, companies, and small independent businessmen will have to borrow money at interest rates between 11 and 13 per cent until they get their rebates-another cost factor to add to inflation.
It would be unparliamentary for me to say the Minister of Finance lied or deliberately misled the House by saying these measures would help conserve gasoline consumption, so I will not say that. But I can say that the minister by sleight of hand did deceive the House into making us believe that energy conservation was a high priority in his mind. I see that on page 32 of the minister's nicely bound budget speech the third paragraph commences:
The increased cost of gasoline resulting from these measures will encourage motorists to make their driving habits more efficient in terms of saving gasoline.
Later on, after a lot of mumbo jumbo about the conservation of fuels, he adds: "improved driving practices-can make significant contributions to needed fuel conservation".

Escalating the price of oil and natural gas is frequently advocated as a means of reducing the rate of growth of consumption of these energy sources. In fact the relationship between the price of energy and its consumption is much too complex to be described by the simple assertion that higher prices result in reduced consumption. Gas prices have gone up from about 39 cents a gallon in the Ottawa area in 1973 to about 72 cents for regular gasoline. During this period there has been no noticeable decline in gasoline consumption. The price of regular gasoline could probably go up to $1.25 or $1.35 before people even considered reducing their purchases.

He had the effrontery to say, on June 23, that the increased cost of gasoline would encourage the use of public transportation. So is he.

True, but we are just talking about his department tonight. It is still in a mess.
