Doctors do not make house calls-I have not found one in years who would make a house call-but they will get refunds for driving to work. Where do they drive to? They drive to their offices, all the expenses for which they can deduct from their income tax. When they do not drive to their office, they drive to the hospital, which is totally maintained at the taxpayers' expense. And for that they are entitled to a gasoline tax rebate. Contrast that with a steelworker in the city of Regina who lives in the south end of the city and who must drive to a steel plant north of the city limits. He will put 6,000 miles a year on his automobile driving to work, the same as the doctor about whom I spoke.
Steelworkers make pretty good money.
Mr. Speaker, back home when we hear noises like the one I just heard from the hon. lady across the way, we say it sounds like a coyote with heartburn.
You are being unfair to coyotes.

The steelworker will put 6,000 miles per year on his car driving to work, and using the figure of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) of 16 miles to the gallon, that is 475 gallons. The ten cents per gallon in this bill will cost $47.50. The five cents per gallon for the increase in the price of oil makes another $23.75. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) said this afternoon, you can bet that with those increases the refiners, wholesalers, bulk dealers and retailers will pass on their percentage mark up, and by the time it goes through the hose into automobile gasoline tanks we will be paying an additional five cents per gallon. The increase in total under this legislation and other legislation resulting from the budget will be 18 cents to 22 cents per gallon. That means $95 to $100 per year more for that steelworker.
All I can say is that there goes that $100 per year tax rebate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) so generously handed out prior to the last federal election. He has taken the whole thing back. However, the real point is that the doctor drives to work in exactly the same way as the steelworker, but the doctor gets the refund. His income is $50,000 to $100,000 per year in Saskatchewan. He receives the refund, but the steelworker who earns $9,000 to $11,000 per year and who drives even more miles to work does not receive it. Any self-respecting Liberal I know in Regina-Lake Centre does not call this just or fair.
Check your figures.
Mr. Speaker, I will check my figure, but not that of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) is seeking the floor to ask a question of the hon. member. This can only be done with the consent of the hon. member.
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I actually should ask a series of questions. I wonder where the hon. member got his inflated idea of doctors' incomes. I wonder where he got the idea that doctors drive to hospitals when they can walk. Does he mean that they could walk when they are answering an emergency call? If they have to go down three times a night, should they walk, or should they drive their cars? I just wonder where the hon. member gets the $50,000 to $100,000 income figures. I would like him to quote figures from some authority.
Hear, hear!
I could not care less if the doctor walks, takes the bus or drives his car. That is not the point.
Let's hope it's your life in doubt.

In fact the doctor who makes emergency calls down to the emergency ward at the hospital in the middle of the night is no different from a good friend of mine who is a foreman at a steel plant. He can be called back to the plant several times a week on emergencies. Doctors can receive refunds on the gas tax, and the steelworker cannot. That is what we are complaining about, and that is what is unfair and unjust.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have compared the figures of the hon. member with my figures, and I think he suffers from an intellectual astigmatism.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!

Since I want to use up my 40 minutes, I hope Your Honour is deducting all these entertaining interjections which I am allowing. I would not want the House not to have the full benefit of my entire 40 minutes.
Let us move to the next group of people whom the Liberals say they feel so strongly for, stand up for, and fight for. Let us consider old age pensioners who may or may not be on a guaranteed income supplement. They do some driving, but not very much. They do things like drive to get their groceries, and to the doctor. The doctor will not come to see them. They drive to see their children and their grandchildren. The Minister of Finance, Mr. Scrooge, and the Minister of National Revenue, Mr. Midas, are trying to chisel old age pensioners out of another $1 or $2 a month with the gasoline tax.
What has the government accomplished? As with the worker, where they will not take back the $100 tax rebate it granted a year ago. Now with the old age pensioners the government can take back that pittance of an escalator clause in the cost of living index which old age pensioners receive. The last increase was, I believe, $2.33 per month. Now the government can take it back from the pensioners with the gasoline tax for the few paltry miles those people drive, and they cannot receive a rebate, but doctors and commercial enterprises can.
People cannot receive the rebate, and I want to say that I am not implying that doctors are not people. My hon. friend across the way is a real fine example of people, but
July 22, 1975

doctors act like corporations and are treated like corporations by this government.
Let us go another step and consider the handicapped. One of my hon. friends to my right raised this matter this afternoon when questioning the Minister of National Revenue. Mr. Scrooge and Mr. Midas sit on the government benches. Mr. Midas, the Minister of National Revenue, said that there is no way he could or would amend this legislation to allow for rebates for the handicapped.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He didn't say that.

That is the way I heard it, and that may or may not be something the governor in council will consider. I have a letter which arrived the other day, and incidentally I wrote to the Minister of Finance on July 9. I have not as yet received an answer. The letter I received is from a senior official in a department or branch of the government of Saskatchewan, and he said that one of his senior staff members is a record review officer and a paraplegic. Other than his wheel chair his only means of transportation is his car. It is a specially equipped automobile. It is the only thing in which he can ride. He is earning a living. He has learned to cope with an affliction with which most of us could not cope. He is not eligible for a rebate, but doctors and commercial enterprises are.
And they laugh.

If there is any conscience whatsoever in the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of Finance, or any other Liberal over there, they will amend their legislation now. They will add a clause so that there will be a clause 47(f), or (h) or whatever so that the handicapped are automatically eligible for the rebate.
Let us look at some more of these injustices. The minister says this measure is aimed at conservation of energy, and that people will shift to other modes of transportation. If he is correct and if that happens to any degree at all, I hope somebody over there can tell me how the minister is going to raise the $350 million to $550 million that he needs. If the legislation has one of the minister's desired effects then it will not bring in the ten cents per gallon. It is just stupid. I have seen the Liberals do some dumb things, Mr. Speaker, but this is the dumbest. That is why it cannot and will not work; that is why it cannot achieve one of the objectives that the minister claims.
I have listened to members talk about transportation in this House and, Mr. Speaker, that subject has been my main concern since I came here in 1968. I say that the alternatives to automobiles are either inaccessible to the mass of working people who will not be eligible for rebate or are of insufficient frequency or capacity, or both. In addition, fares are not low enough to encourage people to shift to another mode of transportation, whether for work or pleasure.
I heard the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) castigate his counterpart in Ontario, saying if he is so concerned why does he not reduce the provincial gasoline tax? As usual, Madam Speaker, Sas-
Excise Tax Act
katchewan is ahead on this, and the NDP is keeping it that way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: That is why everybody is leaving.
Three thousand people have just come back from Alberta.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Or B.C.

One is as good as the other. Madam Speaker, Saskatchewan has forgone ten cents per gallon of its gasoline tax. It has forgone seven cents per gallon directed to the consumer, and another three cents per gallon no longer goes to the provincial treasury; it goes into the automobile insurance fund.
Because they lose money on it.

No, they do not. In B.C., they are still learning. They still have not got rid of all the reactionary capitalists who are fighting public automobile insurance.
I want to remind the hon. member that one of the principles that guides us in automobile insurance in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba is that we say that anybody who would make a profit off the misfortunes of others is immoral.
Oh, oh!

That is why we have an automobile insurance plan in three provinces and, mark my words, it is going to be in another couple pretty soon.
Saskatchewan forgoes nine cents per gallon of the gasoline tax. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said today that if we are so concerned about consumers we should do that, and we did. Now the Minister of Finance takes ten cents per gallon more, and the consumers in Saskatchewan are worse off than before. Saskatchewan has the second lowest gas tax in Canada. Alberta has ten cents per gallon tax and Saskatchewan has 12 cents. In our province we tried to do something to protect consumers from the rising costs of energy, and not only did we get no thanks from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources but the Minister of Finance demanded another ten cents per gallon.
I should now like to turn to unemployment insurance cases. I am not going to talk about unemployment insurance premiums which were mentioned several times in this debate as an additional iniquitous and unfair tax. Unemployment insurance regulations say that, when you are unemployed, to be entitled to benefits you must be fully available for and actively seeking employment. This is where the Liberals forget about the hundreds of thousands of people in this country who live in small cities, towns, and villages and farms, and who are unemployed.
To illustrate-a constituent of mine in the village of Semans, Saskatchewan, who was unemployed last year was told by the UIC that seeking employment in his villages and six neighbouring villages was not sufficient; he should seek employment in the city of Regina. It is a good thing he did not find anything there because it is 80 miles away. It would have been a round trip of 160 miles
29669-13)4

July 22, 1975
Excise Tax Act
per day, and with the additional ten cents per gallon there is no doubt he would be better off unemployed.
The incongruities and inconsistencies in this legislation show just how dumb the government is. There are alternative ways of raising the same amount of money, and I am not disputing the desire of the government to raise several hundreds of millions of dollars for the oil compensation fund. But it does not need to and should not be raising it through people who can least afford to pay it, and exempt the people who can most afford to pay it.
We have suggested several times that the income tax system should be used in one form or other. Let us look at what a thinking Liberal might do.
Where?
There is no such thing.
He is not here tonight.

Wait for it! If you found a thinking large "1" Liberal he would at least have the imagination to say, "Let's put it on the personal income tax". That at least would have some relationship to ability to pay.
The projection of the federal government is that in 1975-76 it will raise $11.4 billion in personal income taxes. To raise that additional $525 million that it says it needs for the oil compensation fund in order to have one price across the country would mean an effective tax rate increase of 5 per cent in the higher brackets. That would raise $500 million or $525 million, and would be a marked improvement over the method chosen in Bill C-66.
Let us go beyond what a thinking Liberal might do- that will take in most of the population of Canada. In 1974 industrial corporations paid $5 billion in corporation income tax. That was an effective tax rate of 32.4 per cent, since their net income before taxes totalled $15.5 billion. A 3.3 per cent increase in the effective tax rate for corporations would give the government the $525 million it says it needs in 12 months. That is a second alternative which could be used for raising this money, and I suggest it is even better than anything a thinking Liberal might do. I will give the Conservatives credit; they might think of the idea, but they might not do it.
Let me propose two other alternatives the government might consider. This afternoon the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands mentioned a surcharge on corporate tax, or a combination of a surcharge on corporate taxes and a higher tax on individuals in higher income brackets. You could raise $525 million if you imposed a surcharge of 4.6 per cent on individual taxable income. You could raise $525 million with a 10 per cent surcharge on corporate taxes payable. Or you could use a combination of these methods, but the point is that they are related to ability to pay. You could and should also exempt those in the low and low-middle income categories, and you could still obtain more than the $525 million you need.
Let me suggest a final, good New Democratic Party socialist alternative. It would be simple to implement and,
in a way, provide corporations with a benefit not available to others.
Yes, the benefit of nationalization.
As at the end of the first quarter of this year there were outstanding on the books of this country over $7 billion in deferred corporate taxes.
That's right, tax everyone out of existence.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member might learn something if he would listen. Everyone knows that those deferred taxes will never be paid. As I say, there were $7 billion worth of deferred taxes on the books, as of March 31 last. They represent an interest free loan from the people of Canada to those corporations, by virtue of the workings of our tax system. Let me recommend this socialist alternative to Bill C-66. Remembering that our constituents must pay between 10 per cent and 12 per cent for mortgages, and that you cannot obtain an individual loan for anything less than 11 per cent or 12 per cent, we should charge the corporations in Canada which owe $7 billion in deferred taxes the low interest rate of 7.5 per cent on those deferred taxes. That is how you could raise your $525 million for the oil fund.
The rest of the citizens of this country cannot defer their taxes. If they could I am sure the Minister of Finance and the Liberal sheep would think of some way to charge them interest. Why not charge the corporations interest? If the party opposite, the so-called party of the just society which supports free enterprise, supports a system of deferred taxes under our tax system, surely it should not support the idea of these deferred taxes being an interest free loan from the public of Canada. I suggest we should be garnering some modest rate of interest; and, at today's rate I think 7.5 per cent on those $7 billion of deferred tax would be a very modest rate. It would not be excessive.
No self-respecting corporation could complain about paying too high an interest rate. They pay much more when they want to build a shopping centre or high rise office building. They will borrow money at 10 per cent or 12 per cent for those; but the people of Canada would only charge them 7.5 per cent on those deferred taxes. If you did that you would have more than you require for the oil compensation program. I suspect that the 7.5 per cent paid on deferred taxes would do more than meet the requirements of the oil compensation fund. It would provide tens of millions of dollars more, which could go to exploration and development of oil, gas, and other energy sources. It would be applauded and accepted by the people generally, and reputable corporations would say it is fair. The disreputable ones, the friends of the Liberal party, may not think it is fair. That's tough.
At one time Liberals and free enterprisers generally used to get some money from the rich and votes from the poor, and promised to protect them from each other. They refined that. Now they give money to the rich and take it from the poor, and still say they are protecting them from each other.
Why did I suggest either a surcharge on the corporate tax-payer in higher income brackets of 10 per cent, or a 7.5

July 22, 1975

per cent interest rate on deferred taxes owing as of March 31 last? What has been happening in this country? I made those suggestions because of the imbalance that has occurred since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his regime came to power in 1968. Madam Speaker, in 1968-69 individual taxpayers in Canada paid 34 per cent of the total tax revenues of the government; corporations paid 20 per cent. There was a spread between 34 per cent and 20 per cent.
By 1970-71, under this just society type of government, individual taxpayers were paying 41 per cent of the total tax bill and the corporate share had dropped to 17 per cent.
By 1972-73 the just society boys with their organizational genius had arranged for the individual taxpayer to pay 43 per cent of the total tax load and the corporations to pay only 16 per cent.
This year there has been a slight recovery. In 1975-76 the individual taxpayer will still carry 41 per cent of the load, but the corporations will have to carry 20 per cent.
By collecting that $525 million from the corporations in 12 months, the government will increase the corporate share of the tax load in this country by another two or three percentage points and make the corporations bear a slightly fairer share of the tax burden of this country.
I have suggested three or four alternatives, one of which even a thinking Liberal could buy. Even if you levied extra tax on personal incomes, that measure would be fairer and more justified than what is proposed in Bill C-66. If the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue and all those seals and sheep on the government side want to get home fast, let them follow my suggestion. It would take only two or three days for the Minister of Finance to bring in a new bill which incorporates any one of my suggestions, and everyone will be surprised at how fast it will pass.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but his allotted time has expired.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this evening in support of the amendment of my leader to give the bill a six months' hoist.
This bill is a rather interesting piece of legislation. It results from a lack of foresight on the part of the government. This lack of foresight is the failure to develop an adequate energy policy and adequate transportation policy.
The bill does four things. First, it takes the excise tax off insulation materials, storm windows and storm doors, something that should have been done a long time ago. While it will only result in a saving of about $25 per home, this portion of the bill is worth while. It is welcomed.
Second, the bill increases the transportation tax, putting a burden on the travelling public. If the money from this transportation tax were used to update landing facilities in the various airports across Canada it would be welcome. If you talk to some of the airline pilots they will tell you that landing facilities at many airports in Canada are inadequate to handle the larger jets, and in some respects
Excise Tax Act
are hazardous. No one would object to a tax on transportation if the moneys were used in the interest of safety for the travelling public. However, I suspect that the money will be used on Mirabel and Pickering airports.
The bill further reduces the tax on domestic wines with more than 7 per cent alcohol by 20 cents per gallon. For wines with less than 7 per cent alcohol, the reduction is 40 cents per gallon. The bill increases the tax on gasoline by ten cents a gallon. It seems that the minister has his priorities mixed. He imposes a ten cents excise tax on a gallon of gasoline and reduces the tax on wines by from 20 to 40 cents per gallon.
Hear, hearl
The minister gave a reason for this in his budget speech.
To get drunk.

I quote from page 26 of the minister's budget speech:
Second, I have also been persuaded by many representations that the increased excise imposed last fall on wine is seriously affecting the domestic wine and grape growing industry of the country. The excise will therefore be reduced to its previous level effective tonight.
One would have thought the minister would have had the foresight to see that this ten cents a gallon tax on gasoline, on top of the other various programs of this government over the years which have led to high rates of inflation, will affect the citizens of this country. Perhaps they more than the wine industry are entitled to a break. After all we can do without wine, but we cannot do without gas.
What is the purpose of this ten cents a gallon tax on gasoline? The minister made two points in his budget. First, he talked about the gap between the compensation payments on oil imports, saying that these had grown rapidly due to the fact that the volume of our oil exports had fallen while our imports had risen. He said at page 32 of his budget speech, and I quote:
Although the increase in the domestic oil price and the forthcoming adjustments in the import compensation program will help, the gap will be substantial.
It is difficult to be precise about the figures because the amount depends upon international prices, export volume and a number of other domestic and international factors. The cost of the subsidy for eastern consumers will be about $1.3 billion this year. The gap between that cost and the export charge revenues is likely to be several hundred million dollars in fiscal 1975-76 and may widen in future.
This tax, according to the minister, will raise approximately $350 million in the balance of this fiscal year. If one relates that to a twelve month period it amounts to almost $420 million. That means the car owners and operators of this country will contribute $420 million in the next year to subsidize the province of Quebec and the mari times.
As a Canadian I believe in an equalized price for gasoline throughout all of Canada. However, like many in western Canada, I feel that equalization should work both ways. When central Canada was paying much less per gallon for gas at the pumps than we in western Canada, there was no talk of such equalization. However, when it appeared that central Canada was going to pay more than
Hear, hear!
A darned good speech!
It shows there is some talent over here-a little originality!

I think the hon. lady was confused. Either the heat had gotten to her or she spoke in jest, because if she had sat back and thought for a moment she would have realized that her remarks about the ostrich school of
July 22, 1975

politics describe the present government exactly. The Liberal government has for many years stuck its head in the sand.
Too bad it wasn't quicksand.

And if she thinks what she calls the big blue ostrich in Queen's Park will be replaced by what she calls a progressive and forward looking bright red Liberal bird of substance, thought, and good government, that big red Liberal bird will be shot down by the gun of the voter, and the bright red plumage will flutter across the countryside of Ontario.
Hooray!

Over the years Canadians have been led to believe there were unlimited supplies of oil and gas in our country. We were led to believe that all we had to do was to go to western Canada or to the Arctic and punch holes down, and the gas and oil would come spouting forth. Suddenly the situation changed overnight. The OPEC nations increased their prices and the government and the National Energy Board began shouting shortages. Any shortages are and will be the fault of the government.
The policy of the government is such that it is discouraging exploration and development. We see oil and gas rigs leaving the country almost every week, together with the skilled crews required to operate those rigs. The rigs should be in western Canada and the northern Arctic, exploring and developing our future supplies of gas and oil. The government should have had the foresight to anticipate a few years ago that we would be faced with shortages. The government should have anticipated that our future reserves lie primarily in northern Canada and that a pipeline down the Mackenzie valley was a necessity. In addition, a land settlement with the native people is necessary before the pipeline can be built with the least amount of social and economic unrest among our native people.
Over the past number of years the government has anticipated nothing; it has merely proceeded in an ad hoc manner. The result was that no attempt was made to deal with the problems and claims of the native people until an application was made to build the pipe line. The Berger commission should have been set up years ago, instead of under the shadow of an energy crisis in the north.
I was interested to hear the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) speak about multinational corporations. It seems to me that many of these multinational corporations are now being looked upon as corporate welfare bums. I point out that without the oil companies we would never have had an oil supply developed in Canada. We would never have had the resources we have had in the past and which we have today.
The government has not told the public that for every gallon of gas sold in Canada the provincial and federal gasoline and excise tax takes anywhere from a low of 41.5 per cent of the basic price of a gallon of gas in Alberta to a high of 60 per cent in the province of Quebec. Neither has it told the public that out of the $8 wellhead price for gas
Adjournment Debate
the federal and provincial governments, through royalties and federal and provincial income taxes, take upwards of 75 per cent. We have developed Petro-Can to solve our problems, but I wonder whether Petro-Can will be able to operate on 25 per cent of the wellhead prices as well as paying its interest on its debt, exploration development and production costs. Looking at the balance sheets of various Crown corporations in Canada today, I doubt it.
I have no hesitation, Madam Speaker, in supporting the amendment of my leader to give this bill a six months' hoist. I feel that if members on the government side of the House have a conscience and have the interests of Canada and their constituents at heart, they should support the amendment. I am looking forward to a summer recess, but I hope that before that time the Minister of Finance will either support the motion of my leader or withdraw the bill. I hope he and members of his cabinet during the summer recess will develop policies in the area of energy, transportation, and economics which will put Canada back on the rails of economic recovery.

Madam Speaker, it certainly gives me great pleasure to be able to speak on the many parts of this devastating bill which will have serious effects on all parts of northern Canada. Most of the people living in communities in my constituency which have roads have anywhere from 500 to 700 miles to drive to reach the main centres in the province. I refer to miners who use their cars to go to work every day. If they want to take their families on a summer vacation they have to travel 700 miles, and will have to pay this ridiculous ten cents a gallon tax to reach a holiday area.
Another problem facing many of the people in the riding of Churchill who live in these remote communities is that there is no public transit system. The people must use their cars if they are to travel at all. Some of these communities comprise as many as 20,000 people. Yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has imposed this ridiculous tax and has burdened the people who are the backbone of our country.
I will now call it ten o'clock, Madam Speaker.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-REASON FOR DETENTION AND INTERROGATION OF DR. FAYEZ SAYEGH, AN ARABIAN DIPLOMAT
IMMIGRATION-REASON FOR DETENTION AND INTERROGATION OF DR. FAYEZ SAYEGH, AN ARABIAN DIPLOMAT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my earnest hope that this will be my last utterance in this august chamber until mid-October. I am also tempted to urge those members who do not stay for this delightful period to follow the advice of Lady Macbeth and to stand not upon the order of their going but to go at once.

July 22, 1975
Adjournment Debate
On May 26 I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) about the detention and interrogation of Dr. Fayez Sayegh at the Toronto International Airport. This distinguished-scholar-statesman who heads the PLO observer delegation to the United Nations was carrying a diplomatic passport from the government of Kuwait. He had been invited to be guest speaker at the annual meeting of the Canadian Arab Federation, a group to which many Canadians of Arab ancestry belong.
The minister, in response, declared that the facts as I had stated them were generally correct. I thought then, and I think now, that we must be extremely careful not to allow our immigration department and its officers be a vehicle of bias in the confrontation in the Middle East.
Members of the Israeli government and other individuals come to Canada frequently to address audiences on their point of view on the current and, alas, continuing conflict in the Middle East. No one ever hears of any spokesman for the Israeli cause having trouble entering Canada, nor should they have. Public discussion on such issues should be welcomed.
But for any Palestinian spokesman to come to Canada to discuss the Palestinian cause and case seems enormously difficult. They are harassed, detained, interrogated, delayed for hours at airports, and embarrassed by immigration officers following them to public meetings and pursuing them with further questions. It is most unfair. It cannot be suggested that to deny Canadians the chance to hear both sides of the issue is the act of a country adopting an even-handed view of the Middle East crisis.
I was also appalled by the suggestion that all members of the PLO are prohibited entry into Canada. Such a view has with it the implication that all PLO and all Palestinians are a threat to the security of Canada.
Dr. Sayegh is a case in point. He is an internationally known scholar, the son of a Presbyterian minister, a man whose knowledge and experience qualified him as one well worth listening to. That such a person with a diplomatic passport should be embarrassed and held up while entering Canada at the invitation of a reputable Canadian organization is an outrage.
We should not be too eager to suppress the right of the long-suffering Palestinians to state their case. The contemplated presence of two or three Palestinian lawyers at the UN crime conference was inflated as a threat to the security of the great city of Toronto and the vast province of Ontario. I found such assertions as incredible as the government's response to the pressures and proclamations against Palestinian attendance at a UN conference to which they had the right to come.
This is not the place to analyze the government's decision on the proposed Toronto conference, but I doubt if world peace of Canadian foreign policy will be enhanced thereby.
It is to be hoped that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration will realize some of the delicacy and sensitivity of the problems of the Middle East, the chief of which is the fate of the Palestinian people.

I was a little disturbed at some replies I received to an order paper question. Contrary to the minister's oral reply, the answers denied that Dr. Sayegh had been detained and interrogated. The same blanket of denial was drawn over inquiries regarding Palestinian and other Arab labour leaders who entered the country through Montreal recently. My information leaves me no doubt about the incidents. These people did not receive a warm welcome or routine entry into this country. The former need not be expected; but all Palestinians ought not to be made special cases and presented with the presumption that their visit is designed to be hurtful to Canada's security.

speakeroldname: Mr. William Rompkey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: IMMIGRATION-REASON FOR DETENTION AND INTERROGATION OF DR. FAYEZ SAYEGH, AN ARABIAN DIPLOMAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) raised this matter in the House on May 26, 1975, he was informed that when Dr. Sayegh sought entry he admitted membership in the Palestine Liberation Organization and that this, under Canadian law, made him inadmissible to Canada. The policy of the Department of Manpower and Immigration, in cases where a prohibited person is invited to speak by a reputable Canadian organization, is to allow that person temporary entry under the minister's permit if it is considered that there will be no threat to Canada's national security. This is called the Nicholson policy.
All that can be added, Mr. Speaker, is to assure hon. members that no slur was meant to be cast on a foreign diplomat attached to the UN but that the action taken was required by his admitted membership in the PLO.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-AVAILABILITY OF CORPORATION'S EDUCATIONAL FILMS TO SCHOOLS- GOVERNMENT ACTION
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-AVAILABILITY OF CORPORATION'S EDUCATIONAL FILMS TO SCHOOLS- GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second parliament in which I have tried to have CBC broadcasting educational films provided to schools and universities across Canada. Actually for four years school boards and universities have been attempting to obtain these films. The stalling by the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) and the CBC in respect of the solution of this problem has now become absolutely ridiculous.
It is disappointing that the minister is not here to answer questions on such an important subject. The question of the CBC providing educational films to school boards and universities throughout Canada is of major importance and is a subject on which I hope the government can throw some light tonight.
There are certain problems in respect of the present Copyright Act. In the last parliament I made the following suggestions for amendments to the present act:
(1)	copying and duplicating should be allowed for, subject to suitable safeguards to protect the legitimate interests of the creator and publisher;
(2)	In the case of broadcast programs of an educational nature there should be recognition of the need to record them for playback within a limited period. In this situation the tape recording may be used to meet timetabling requirements without royalty payment; (3) transmission of copyright material through closed-circuit television systems should be subject to reasonable royalties and fees in terms of the specific target audience.
School boards and teachers have experienced distress-
July 22, 1975

in the last four years
-because of current inadequacy in legislation and failure to reach agreement at the federal level. The Canadian Teachers' Federation has presented a number of briefs in this regard and I believe note should be made of some of the comments which have been made public. One is as follows:
"Since there appears to be widespread expectation that the Copyright Act will be substantially revised in the near future, CTF believes that such a revision could not be long delayed and that it is of the utmost importance that all interested parties should have the opportunity to participate in the revision. The brief complains that CBC program materials are being handed over to an American-dominated private company for distribution on a profit making basis".
Here is a quotation from a statement by .. . the CTF president:
"I am pleased to have a strong mandate to secure the full and free use in Canadian schools of educational programs developed with the support of public moneys . .. we will present our views regarding the difficulties being experienced with video taping of school telecasts for viewing at a more convenient time because of the present copyright laws as well as certain contractual arrangements at the CBC".
In the last parliament I presented a bill, an act to amend the Broadcasting Act. The government agreed at that time to allow the bill to go to committee. We finally got it to committee, and one afternoon at 3.30 p.m. seven Conservatives arrived to discuss the bill. The only other people in attendance were a couple of CBC officials and the chairman of the committee, who is a Liberal. We did not have a quorum and therefore we could not discuss this bill in committee. People in the educational field had come to Ottawa to participate in this committee meeting, they came from B.C., Nova Scotia and all across Canada. They were insulted, and they felt they were treated with contempt by the Liberal government and the Liberal members of that committee.
I was hoping that this bill could be sent to committee in this parliament because obviously the Secretary of State, who is responsible for the CBC, is not capable of finding a solution to this problem.
Recently I received a letter from the Canadian School Trustees Association. The executive director wrote:
Your bill has been labelled "simplistic" and that is a great compliment. I am becoming tired and angry with people stating that things are complex, and no simple solution can be found.
It is very strange that the Secretary of State and the CBC cannot find some solution to this problem after four years. There has been an exchange of correspondence such as I have never seen in my life. In the last parliament every member of parliament received letters from school teachers, school children, school trustees, associations and universities giving support to this bill, and all the cabinet members were bombarded with mail. So was the Secretary of State and the CBC. But here we are going through the same exercise in the thirtieth parliament. You can see, Madam Chairman, how ridiculous this is.
A couple of weeks ago I asked the minister what he was doing about the problem. I received the biggest run around that I have ever witnessed in my life on what they are doing to Canada's educational system in regard to this problem in providing CBC educational films in Canadian schools. We are talking about six million school children and about every school and university in Canada. It is absolutely ridiculous that the government has not found a solution to the problem by now. Four years is more than enough time.
Adjournment Debate
I received one letter from the minister back in 1973, and he indicated the following:
CBC is conscious of the desirability of making an early statement on the matter of providing some programs for use in schools. However, the problem is complex and it is not known yet whether release of a significant number of programs will be possible.
As soon as it is able to do so, the corporation will be making a statement. If the study proceeds as at present, this may be by the beginning of the next school year, or shortly thereafter.
This letter is dated July, 1973, and this should have been solved in 1974. Here we are in the middle of 1975, and we are still talking about the problem. Now the Schoolteachers Association and the School Trustees Association and all the schools across Canada are going to start another letter exchange, writing to all their members of parliament, the Secretary of State, and the CBC to see if they can get them off their butts to do something about this problem.
This problem has reached ridiculous proportions. I cannot find the words to explain it, and I hope the parliamentary secretary has some reasonable explanation tonight.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gustave Blouin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-AVAILABILITY OF CORPORATION'S EDUCATIONAL FILMS TO SCHOOLS- GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) it is fairly common knowledge that CBC has been carrying out a detailed study of the problems associated with a plan to release a large number of its television and radio programs for use by non profit organizations and by individuals following broadcast.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) has already mentioned that CBC has accepted in principle the responsibility of meeting the heavy demands for its programs from schools, service clubs and church groups, demands which originate in all parts of Canada. On the basis of its studies up to that time CBC included in its estimates last fall an amount sufficient to enable it to get started with its further use project in the current fiscal year. Funds slightly in excess of $1 million were made available by the government.
The Secretary of State has been informed by CBC that two or three important issues are still under consideration. For example, the corporation has been studying the impact of its further use project on the private Canadian non theatrical film industry. It is quite possible that the release of CBC's programs into a limited market may have a detrimental effect on a part of the film industry and that this, in turn, may adversely influence other initiatives of the department to assist the growth of the Canadian film industry generally.
In itself concern for the private companies is not a reason to delay the inauguration of the further use project, but CBC feels that the situation should be carefully explored. The corporation will begin further use project distribution as soon as possible. It is aware of the high expectations held by many, and is determined that the project will be successful.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISMISSAL OF MESSRS. CHO, CHEW AND McGUIRE BY CN TELECOMMUNICATIONS- REQUEST FOR REPORT
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISMISSAL OF MESSRS. CHO, CHEW AND McGUIRE BY CN TELECOMMUNICATIONS- REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise tonight to speak on a matter I raised in this House yesterday afternoon regarding the dismissal of three employees from the Canadian National Telecommunications system, Mr. Cho, Mr. Chew and Mr. McGuire.
After arriving back in Ottawa Sunday night I made sure I was in my office early Monday morning. I telephoned the office of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), the office of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier), and the office of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), and gave them notice of my question. I spent them a copy of a letter I had received from Mr. Horbulyk, who is the acting chairman of the Canadian Telecommunications division of CB of RT and GW. I sent the ministers a copy of the grievance which had been filed by the union on behalf of Mr. Young Cho. I told them that I wanted to ask this question in the House. I thought it was a very serious matter, and I hoped by giving them this notice we could receive some proper answers and take away a shadow which has been cast over these three men.
The minister in his answer said that he immediately got in touch with the president of CN and he was supposed to have another discussion with him. He also stated:
I know they have been following this practice for a very long time. However, this practice worries me as much as the hon. member.
It certainly worries me, Madam Speaker, and I was quite pleased with the answer. I knew the minister was concerned and viewed this as a very serious question that he wanted to discuss with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and cabinet. I did not ask a supplementary, fully expecting that today in this House we would have an answer from the minister which, if not complete and detailed, would at least give some idea of what had happened. Today in answer to the same question I received the same answer although I have not had a chance to check it over.
I find it unbelievable that the government, which seemed so concerned, and the Minister of Transport who was shaken by the matter, cannot get an answer from the president of Canadian National Railways. Certainly the president should be able to have an answer for the minister by the next day. If he had said today that somebody was on vacation I could understand that at this time of year, but we received no explanation.
The shadow that has fallen on these men scares me. Three people have been dismissed by a large corporation and not told the reason. When asked by the union, the management stated that they are not at liberty to say why Mr. Cho had been dismissed. The union explained that this left Mr. Cho in a very strange position, and management agreed and said had Mr. Cho worked in a non-security area his dismissal would have been unnecessary. One immediately assumes then that this man is a security risk, and this is the shadow cast on the other men. If they are, we should know, and we should know why they were hired in the first place. They must have had to go through some clearance in order to be hired.
Mr. Cho has been offered another job in the company in a non-secure area. He says he sees no reason why he is
regarded as a security risk. He was cleared by the United States army when, as a captain in the South Korean army, he was sent to Texas for training.
The thing that frightens me is that three union clauses were violated. Clause 1 states in part:
An employee... will not be disciplined or discharged until his case has been thoroughly reviewed.
That did not happen in this case, and this is one of the grievances filed. Clause 2 states in part:
... and will be advised of the reasons for such review.
Clause 3 states in part:
... an employee will not be held out of service pending rendering of decision except in case of a dismissable offence.
That clause was also broken by the government. When a large company like CN can violate a union agreement, that means any company in this country can do the same. The government should take swift action. I am sure I gave the parliamentary secretary some information tonight. We have not got complete answers yet, but tomorrow this House should have a full explanation from the minister of why the rights of three people in Canada have been violated by a company associated with the government.
The president of CNR, who has been approached by a minister of the Crown, should be fired if he cannot tell the House within 24 or 48 hours why three employees were dismissed in an underhanded way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISMISSAL OF MESSRS. CHO, CHEW AND McGUIRE BY CN TELECOMMUNICATIONS- REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has indicated to the House that he is most certainly concerned about the problem raised yesterday by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) and he contacted the president of the CNR immediately upon learning of the situation. I hope my hon. friend opposite will give us until tomorrow. I cannot account for the delays, but I understand they are legitimate and that the minister will have the opportunity for further discussions! with the president of the CNR on this matter.
The minister is aware of the serious implications of the practice involved here, and I believe he indicated to the House yesterday that he intends to raise the matter with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the cabinet.
I am advised that .the three employees involved were offered other positions because they did not meet the requirements of their positions, but if I understand my hon. friend correctly that is not his information. I will check that out myself; I believe it refers to only two of them. I can assure my hon. friend that his concern is shared by the minister.
I am sure the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta knows, from his experience in this chamber, that no member is more deeply concerned for the rights of working men and women of this country than the present Minister of Transport. I hope the hon. member will allow us a little more time to provide an answer that is acceptable.
